title: Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents
raw_text: As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale , from systems of record to systems of action , and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows , the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s. Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate , gVisor , and OpenRL , three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE . Each project is now working through CNCF Sandbox onboarding with community maintainers and independent build infrastructure, and gVisor is on a path toward Incubation. These releases deliver an open stack that runs on any Kubernetes cluster, on any cloud, across CPUs, GPUs, or TPUs, by: Scaling isolated agent environments without idle compute overhead with Agent Substrate (now 1.0 and GA on GKE): Agents execute code or tests for a few seconds, then wait on model turns, external APIs, or human input. Keeping a dedicated container alive during those pauses ties up memory and compute. Agent Substrate decouples stateful agent sessions and identities from active compute, snapshotting idle agents to storage and restoring them in under 500 milliseconds to run millions of sandboxes at 10x container density. Isolating untrusted code within a sandbox with gVisor : Agents routinely generate and run unreviewed code and external packages, making standard containers that share a host Linux kernel a security risk. gVisor isolates generated code inside a lightweight userspace application kernel at container packing density on any Linux node. Distributing post training and serving efficiently with OpenRL : Training agents with reinforcement learning (RL) gives builders an open loop to learn across millions of parallel sandboxed rollouts. OpenRL orchestrates self-hosted RL post-training loops in plain Python on Kubernetes. Scale fully isolated agent environments with Substrate Agents need isolated compute resources and strict access boundaries, yet spend most of their time waiting: executing code for a few seconds, then pausing while a model reasons or a human responds. They need a discrete identity and central enforcement point to ensure the agent only accesses authorized tools and services without holding sensitive keys. In standard Kubernetes, giving every active agent its own Pod locks up memory and CPU while the agent sits idle, forces the control plane to track millions of persistent objects it was never designed to hold, and ties identities directly to Pods. At the same time, identities are intrinsically tied to Kubernetes Pods, adding exponential complexity for controlling access and secrets. Agent Substrate solves this by separating the stateful agent from the underlying compute: Actors hold each agent's memory, files, and discrete identity. Workers are reusable execution sandboxes drawn from a warm Kubernetes pool. Gateways enforce inbound and outbound access control and inject secrets based on Actor identity, keeping sensitive keys out of the agent environment. When an agent pauses to wait on a model turn or tool call, Agent Substrate snapshots the agent’s memory and files to storage and immediately returns the Worker to the warm pool. When the next request arrives, Agent Substrate restores the Actor onto any available Worker in under 500 milliseconds and picks up right where it left off. Think of it as a hotel room rather than a house: you don't keep a room when you leave town, and a new room is ready when you come back. Agent Substrate decouples stateful Actors and policy Gateways from a warm pool of Kubernetes Workers, restoring idle sessions in under 500 milliseconds. Since public development started in May 2026, the Agent Substrate project has grown to more than 100 contributors. Early design partners like Nous Research are building Hermes Enterprise on it , and it already powers other CNCF projects like kagent . Further, reaching the 1.0 milestone shows that Agent Substrate can accept production workloads across millions of sandboxes, achieving 10x the density of standard container runtimes, and performing more than 500 suspend and resume activations per second . Underneath, you can choose Cloud Hypervisor microVMs or gVisor as your isolation boundary without changing how you manage agent lifecycles. Because Agent Substrate runs standard OCI containers, it works out of the box with Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, stateful coding environments, and productivity agents. With today's general availability of Agent Substrate on GKE , you can run this runtime as a managed capability on Google Cloud or deploy the open-source code on any Kubernetes cluster. For teams that want a dedicated microVM compute service through an API without having to manage clusters, Agent Substrate complements Agent Compute Engine , our Titanium microVM service that features fast hibernation and parallel environment-forking for evaluation and RL pipelines. SPIRITT is building their SPIRITT Workspace, a platform where agents run real work autonomously while humans collaborate to steer the vision, on top of Agent Substrate on GKE. ”At SPIRITT, every customer gets an autonomous AI workspace where an agent, or a whole swarm of agents, builds, runs, and ships real work across the organization, from code and development cycles to marketing and operations. Agent Substrate on GKE gives us the security isolation to let agents execute code safely, the extensibility to plug in our own runtime, and the density to run every customer's agents economically at scale." - Tamir Magen, CEO, SPIRITT Isolate untrusted agent code with gVisor When agents shift from systems of record to systems of action, they run generated shell commands and unreviewed packages. Standard containers share the host Linux kernel with every other workload on the node, which is a risky bet for untrusted code. Hardware microVMs offer a strong boundary, and Agent Substrate supports them natively. Many teams also need strong isolation that runs at container density across any standard Linux instance, even when bare metal or nested virtualization isn't available. gVisor provides that isolation through a lightweight application kernel written in Go. Sitting between the container and the host OS, gVisor intercepts and handles application system calls in userspace so untrusted code never talks directly to the host kernel. Open sourced by Google in 2018, gVisor runs millions of sandboxes every day underneath GKE Sandbox and Cloud Run. Outside Google, Anthropic and OpenAI use it to contain code execution, Modal and Snowflake run their execution sandboxes on it, and Ant Group and Tencent run it in production at scale. Three capabilities make gVisor a natural fit for agent fleets: Container density and flexible memory: Unlike VMs that preallocate fixed blocks of RAM, gVisor keeps a container process model where memory scales up and down with the workload, packing more agents onto every node and lowering your cost per agent. Native GPU, TPU, and snapshot support: gVisor supports GPUs , TPUs , and checkpoint/restore natively, so agents can access accelerators inside the sandbox and pause when idle. Runs anywhere Linux runs: Because it doesn't require nested virtualization, gVisor deploys identically across any cloud or local Linux node. Northflank , for example, uses gVisor to sandbox GPU workloads when nested virtualization isn't available. Donating gVisor to the CNCF clears a longstanding performance barrier for the community. Sandboxed infrastructure providers, including Google, all carry host kernel patches that bring gVisor's I/O performance close to that of native Linux, but upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor. Moving to neutral CNCF governance opens the path to upstreaming those kernel optimizations, so every builder gets near native performance out of the box. With this move, Ant Group, Modal, and Tines have committed to join gVisor's maintainers , with OpenAI, Tencent, and NVIDIA continuing their contributions. Scale RL post training on Kubernetes with OpenRL The sandbox that runs your agent in production is the exact same environment you need to train an agent with reinforcement learning. Today, most frontier capability gains come from RL post-training: running millions of multiturn rollouts inside real tools, scoring the outcomes, and updating model weights. Building that loop yourself usually means forking a monolithic RL framework and debugging distributed weight transfers before you ever touch your training algorithm. OpenRL brings a clean, self-hosted Python post-training loop directly to your Kubernetes cluster, with: Simple Python primitives: Write your training loop using four clean primitives ( sample , forward_backward , optim_step , and save_state ) through a Tinker compatible API while keeping your weights and data on your own cluster. Existing tinker-cookbook recipes run unchanged, supporting both LoRA adapters and full parameter fine-tuning. Pluggable engines and Kubernetes scheduling: OpenRL uses Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to partition your accelerator pool and orchestrate RL work on the shared pool. Its pluggable architecture uses standard engines, including PyTorch / AutoModel for training and vLLM for sampling, with Gemma and Qwen validated out of the box, and with TPU support on the roadmap. OpenRL also pairs with llm-d , the CNCF distributed inference and RL project founded by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA that recently reached 1.0 , to keep your accelerators busy across both phases of RL. Here, llm-d provides: Prefix-aware rollout routing: The llm-d router routes multiturn rollouts to samplers that already hold matching KV cache prefixes, cutting redundant prefill compute. GPU time-slicing between training and sampling: In RL training, samplers and trainers take turns, leaving one set of chips idle while the other works. OpenRL uses llm-d time-slicing to share the same physical GPUs between sampling and training, reclaiming idle accelerator cycles the same way Agent Substrate reclaims idle CPU and RAM. OpenRL drives plain Python RL loops on Kubernetes, running episodes inside Agent Substrate sandboxes while llm-d routes rollouts and time slices accelerators. OpenRL is the newest layer of this stack by a wide margin. It started in February as a research preview, and we are bringing it to the CNCF early on purpose. Its north star is one recipe for any model on any accelerator, and no single company can get there alone. To get there, you need the people building accelerators (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and TPUs), inference engines ( llm-d , vLLM , SGLang ), training frameworks, and open-weight models starting with Gemma and Qwen. Setting up neutral CNCF governance before the design hardens makes room for everyone to build it together. Why the CNCF, and why now Improving the security and efficiency of AI agents takes joint design across the runtime, scheduler, compiler, and silicon. The past year made the need for affordable, isolated sandboxing and open post-training infrastructure exceedingly clear. Donating Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL to the CNCF reaffirms Google’s commitment to open collaboration and co-investment. Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally. We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes. Come find us at KubeCon Join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City (November 9 to 12) across our sessions and at the Google Cloud booth to learn more about Agent Substrate, OpenRL, and gVisor. You will also hear soon from community partners including Modal, Anyscale, and Tecton on what this open stack means for their agentic workloads. In the meantime, here is where to start: Follow the CNCF Sandbox applications: gVisor #521 , Agent Substrate #523 , and OpenRL #518 , alongside cohort peer KubeRay #525 Kick the tires: ate.dev , gvisor.dev , and openrl.dev Run agents on GKE today: Agent Substrate on GKE , and GKE Sandbox Read the deep dives: Agent Substrate on GKE , gVisor's move to the CNCF , and Introducing OpenRL

title: Helping you build and defend at machine-speed in the agentic era
raw_text: As both a frontier lab and the operator of the world's most comprehensive threat intelligence network, Google occupies a unique vantage point: We see exactly how Large Language Models are engineered, and how adversaries are targeting them in the wild. Passive defense is no longer viable. Allowing rapid, ungoverned adoption of autonomous systems into traditional workflows can lead to critical security incidents. At the Google Cloud Security Summit, we are sharing updates on how we are helping organizations build securely, secure systems, and defend at machine speed in the agentic era. Building securely in the agentic era Agentic coding tools have dramatically accelerated software delivery, but human review can’t keep up with machine-speed commits and unvetted dependencies. Because autonomous agents are now part of the supply chain, blind trust can turn them into direct backdoors for attackers. Our approach to securing the development lifecycle builds native, real-time guardrails in the integrated development environment (IDE), unifies asset graphs across code and identity and access management (IAM,) and verifies models to weed out logic flaws before code merges. CodeMender: Frontier cyber with enterprise control As software-driven threats continue to escalate, our autonomous code-security agent CodeMender helps organizations find and fix code vulnerabilities at machine speed. It can eliminate manual triage bottlenecks while deeply embedding security in the software development lifecycle. CodeMender works with multiple models, including Gemini 4 Argon , that can bring state-of-the-art cybersecurity capabilities. These include identifying previously-unknown vulnerabilities, and generating tested patches before they can be exploited. Most recently, Wiz used Gemini 4 Argon along with other models to identify and help remediate core PHP vulnerabilities that affected 70% of websites . Gemini 4 Argon made a notable contribution to finding the vulnerability, developing a likely exploit path, detecting attacks, and validating the patch. Currently in preview, CodeMender delivers new capabilities for secure isolation and flexible scanning: Secure autonomous remediation : CodeMender isolates vulnerability verification and exploit simulation inside your choice of operating system-level sandbox or isolated virtual machine, and adds human-in-the-loop checks for local write and command execution helping to reduce the risks of malicious exploits and zero-day testing gone awry. Flexible scanning modes : CodeMender now allows you to scan a specific folder, entire repository, or only modified files since the last scan so you have fine grain control on how many files to scan to optimize for scanning speed and costs. Since the CodeMender preview became available in July, hundreds of customers have used CodeMender to help them find and fix vulnerabilities at machine speed. “As adversaries attack at machine speed, Google’s Fairwind Program helps us keep pace with our application security. Our early evaluation of CodeMender shows the potential to reduce vulnerability discovery time by over 95%, while keeping expert validation and remediation under human oversight,” said Ivan Fontarensky, CTO Cybersecurity Services, Thales Group. “IDC research finds that nearly 40% of enterprises add vulnerabilities faster than they can remediate them. Detection without remediation only adds to developer workloads,” said Katie Norton, research director, Cloud Security, IDC. “CodeMender solves this by pairing exploitability validation with deployable code fixes, driving the continuous, verified patching required as exploitation timelines compress.” Securing workloads everywhere When autonomous workloads transition to production, the threat landscape shifts entirely. Adversaries target your plumbing — credentials, data boundaries, and integrations that connect agents to the enterprise. Once inside, attackers exploit over-privileged credentials and unsegmented environments to move laterally across enterprise data boundaries. To eliminate these flat-trust architectures, Google Cloud delivers a unified framework of foundational security and governance controls for agents everywhere they run. Whether your agents are operating on the Gemini platform, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and Cloud Run, the new Agent Compute Engine , or are coordinating across multi-cloud environments — they are bound by the same rigorous enterprise controls. To enforce our agents everywhere framework at the transaction level, we are introducing critical identity, network, and content controls: Auth Manager (Agent Identity) : Centralizes credential management inside a Google-managed vault governed by IAM. Now generally available, Auth Manager automates OAuth 2.0/PKCE flows and refreshes user-delegated tokens to minimize consent fatigue and reduce credential theft. Alongside Auth Manager, Agent Identity JWT support , now in preview, issues standard OIDC tokens, allowing agents to authenticate securely across AWS, Azure, on-premises backends, and MCP servers without static, long-lived API keys. Identity-based VPC Service Controls : Reinforcing perimeter defenses against data exfiltration, VPC-SC ingress and egress rules now support IAM roles , generally available, and Workload Identity Federation for GKE , in preview, enabling security teams to enforce granular, identity-based perimeter boundaries across enterprise GKE clusters without complex, manual exceptions. Model Armor custom topic detector : This new enhancement, available in preview, enables you to enforce topic adherence for agents. You can define custom prompt-based rules to identify on-topic and off-topic interactions. Tailored for industry use cases in healthcare, insurance, and retail, it keeps your agent conversations focused, compliant, and secure. Advanced network threat protection: Building on Cloud NGFW Enterprise’ IPS capabilities, you can now protect workloads with the new Cloud NGFW advanced malware sandbox , generally available, enabled by Palo Alto Networks WildFire, streamline firewall operations using Cloud NGFW project-level resources , generally available, and automate exploit protection with Cloud Armor managed rules , available in preview, backed by Thales Imperva’s global threat intelligence that scans 1.5 trillion monthly web requests. Defending at machine-speed Attackers are integrating advanced capabilities across their operational lifecycles to achieve unprecedented scale and velocity. To defeat autonomous, multi-agent threats, we must empower defenders with agentic, intelligence-driven operations to neutralize adversaries in minutes, not days. Modern SOCs require autonomous investigation, detection, and response powered by planetary-scale infrastructure: Continuous monitoring catches live compromises at the workload layer and feeds telemetry directly into the Wiz Security Graph. Google Threat Intelligence telemetry is codified directly into the runtime logic of defensive models, triggering automated agentic threat hunts that reconstruct process trees and isolate threats in real time. Autonomous agents analyze complex alerts, run correlation queries across multi-vendor telemetry in sub-second timeframes, and present clear mitigation actions for strategic human sign-off. Of course, deploying autonomous technology is only half the battle; teams also need the right operational frameworks to wield it effectively. To help you evolve your cyber defense operations, Mandiant Transformation Services experts can modernize your operating models to maximize the benefits of these advanced technologies. By refining processes and workforce skills with frontline best practices, Mandiant enables your organization to proactively mitigate threats and ensure business continuity during a breach. Better together: Wiz and Google Cloud Delivering end-to-end defense requires extending these native platform controls into multi-cloud environments where organizations run diverse tooling. Together, Wiz and Google Cloud are combining deep autonomous application understanding, connected security context, and threat intelligence to help organizations innovate securely and stay ahead of emerging threats. Recent highlights include: Securing autonomous workloads wherever you build and run with Wiz: As organizations build and scale with Google Cloud and Gemini platform, Wiz protects autonomous applications across their entire lifecycle from code to runtime. Wiz discovers and maps autonomous applications, agents, and infrastructure, deeply analyzing the application itself, including its purpose, capabilities, and permissions, to uncover hidden risks. Combined with the context of the Wiz Security Graph, this surfaces complex attack paths and runtime threats, empowering teams to prioritize risk and innovate with confidence. Securing code at machine speed with Wiz AI SAST : Now in preview, Wiz AI Static Application Security Testing (SAST) uses agentic reasoning to understand how an application behaves and surface complex business logic flaws. Grounded in Wiz Research and powered by our proprietary Atlas harness, Wiz AI SAST correlates code weaknesses with infrastructure context on the Wiz Security Graph so teams can prioritize the risks that matter most. Exploitable attack paths can then be remediated at machine speed using our Green Agent and CodeMender. Strengthening threat defense together with Wiz plus Google Security Operations : Wiz Defend and Google Security Operations now work from a shared data model, giving security operations teams the flexibility to investigate threats in either platform. Improvements include a dedicated Wiz Content Pack in Google Security Operations, Wiz Blue Agent investigation analysis in Google Security Operations, and bi-directional syncing between the platforms for a streamlined analyst experience. Additionally, Wiz Defend now integrates with Google Threat Intelligence, bringing the latest insights and frontline intelligence directly into Wiz. Protecting under-resourced organizations with Scan for Good : A joint initiative launched by Google DeepMind and Wiz, Scan for Good brings the power of autonomous technology coupled with human security researchers to under-resourced organizations, including public services, critical infrastructure, and non-profits. In its first month, this initiative has used Argon to help more than 50 public service organizations and critical infrastructure providers find and remediate critical exposures. Turning the advantage back to the builders and defenders Securing the agentic era requires evolving operational models, enforcing secure-by-design pipelines, and taking direct action against malicious infrastructure. At Google, our responsibility extends to disrupting adversaries at the source: Tracking bad actors targeting Google Cloud environments and permanently disabling their infrastructure. Engineering specialized defensive architectures with Google DeepMind, including models trained specifically for high-stakes cybersecurity and automated code analysis. Feeding frontline threat intelligence back into model alignment and classifier training to neutralize emerging attack vectors before they materialize. By establishing native pipeline defenses, dismantling flat trust architectures, and deploying machine-speed operations, enterprises can turn the AI advantage back to defenders. Join us at the Google Cloud Security Summit to explore these capabilities and learn how to secure your organization in the agentic era.

title: Highlights and reflections from Google Public Sector Summit: Where mission meets moonshot
raw_text: Over 2,700 government leaders, innovators, and industry partners convened across two-days at our Google Public Sector Summit in Washington D.C. where we explored the theme, “Where mission meets moonshot.” We were honored to bring together leaders who are driving impact in the agentic era and leveraging agents to help boost productivity, drive innovation, and transform how services are delivered. Let’s take a closer look at the sessions, speakers, demos, and activations throughout the event that showcased how leaders across education and government are collaborating with Google Public Sector to turn their moonshot aspirations into secure, scaled, real-world mission outcomes. Driving impact together In our morning keynote, CEO of Google Public Sector, Karen Dahut unpacked the event theme and shared how organizations like NASA, NOAA, The Department of War, The Department of Energy, The State of Connecticut, The U.S. Army, Case Western Reserve University, and more are collaborating with Google to drive impact in the agentic era. Karen underscored the importance of leading boldly, building with and for your people, and scaling for impact. Thomas Kurian , CEO of Google Cloud, reinforced our commitment and shared the latest innovations across our integrated and secure stack including Gemini for government services , purpose-built for public sector missions. He also shared additional announcements including the Wiz Red, Green, and Blue agents which are now available within Wiz for Gov, Wiz’s FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment, and how we are bringing enterprise search capabilities to Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud for air-gapped deployments . Chris Hein , Field CTO of Google Public Sector, shared a live product demonstration that showcased Google’s technology in action. Attendees had the opportunity to hear from leaders Michael P. Duffey , Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, and Ed Forst, Administrator for the General Services Administration, who shared how they are applying technology to transform their missions and power their moonshots. Through partnership and powerful technology, we are creating impact at scale by transforming services, strengthening security, and improving outcomes. Dedicated programming for the agentic era During our Cloud Talks session, attendees heard from Elizabeth Moon, Managing Director of Customer Engineering for Google Public Sector, as she hosted a series of talks across critical pillars of public sector transformation. Presentations highlighted infrastructure for the agentic era led by Rich Sanzi, VP/GM for Accelerated Computing Systems at Google Cloud; building safely with Google’s agentic capabilities led by Michael Gerstenhaber , VP of Product Management for Gemini; and implementing proactive defense at planet-scale led by Sandra Joyce , VP of Google Threat Intelligence. Attendees also heard from dozens of customer and partner speakers during our breakout panels hosted by Google Public Sector leaders Ron Bushar, Tony Orlando, and Elizabeth Moon, as well as our lightning talks and closed-door birds of a feather discussions on topics including tokenomics, migration, and compliance. Alongside our customers and partners, we showcased how agents are transforming every facet of the public sector, from accelerating scientific breakthroughs, advancing healthcare outcomes, improving service delivery, strengthening national security, and more. Over the course of the event, we offered specialized programming and engagement opportunities for national security and defense leaders. Through our Partner Connect programming, we shared how we are scaling our impact through a thriving, highly capable partner community and introduced enhanced partner initiatives focused on fostering deeper collaboration, supercharging frontline adoption, and expanding mission delivery capabilities across our valued partner network. Hands-on innovation with Google Public Sector The Mission Exchange served as our interactive showfloor centerpiece, bringing multi-agent coordination to life with our flagship Emergency Response Simulation, as well as live demos that showcased our full-stack innovations encompassing everything from planet-scale infrastructure to leading models and agentic platforms. We hosted 19 lightning talks in the Mission Exchange, featuring customer, partner and Google experts who shared live demos and showcased real-world mission-ready solutions. Attendees also had the opportunity to join our technical hands-on labs including “Getting Started with Gemini” and “Build Gemini Agents: From Prompt to Prototype” where they built functional mission-ready agents with Google Cloud. What’s your moonshot? I was honored to lead our closing session, “What’s your moonshot?” where we brought together visionary leaders Adam McCarthy (The White House), Laura Baker (NYS Board of Elections), and Barry J. Schindler (USPTO) to explore practical strategies for fostering a culture of courageous problem-solving and applying technology to supercharge ambition and ingenuity in entirely new ways. As we look ahead, I want to leave you with one question: “What’s your moonshot?” Answering this question will require bold leadership, ambition, and courage; it will require partnership and collaboration across teams and organizations; and technology that can help amplify capacity and potential. Leading in the agentic era means being comfortable with stepping into the unknown. title: Introducing Compute Engine API multi-versioning: Predictable evolution without breaking production
raw_text:
Ready to modernize your infrastructure without risking production stability? API multi-versioning for Compute Engine, now in general availability, helps you do just that. With date-based API versions, Compute Engine can now regularly deliver modern API semantics, stronger resilience defaults, and improved developer experience while preserving the rock-solid stability of the /v1 API. For more than a decade, the Google Compute Engine /v1 API has served as the foundational control plane for millions of virtual machines, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters, and large-scale AI infrastructure. For platform teams and developers who build on Google Cloud, that single /v1 endpoint delivered an extraordinary promise: write your integration once, and trust that it will keep running year after year. Yet as cloud architectures have grown in scale and sophistication, infrastructure teams have faced a growing tension. On one hand, mission-critical production workloads require absolute API stability and strict backward compatibility. On the other hand, customers want faster access to safer security defaults, stronger regional resilience, machine-readable error models, and modern, declarative-friendly APIs, but introducing these improvements in place risks disrupting existing automation. The new versioning model helps avoid that disruption by giving you the flexibility to adopt modern semantics on your own schedule without touching your production workloads. Date-based API versions for Compute Engine Historically, Compute Engine relied on channel-based versioning (CBV) with three long-lived channels: /v1 (generally available), /beta , and /alpha . Because /v1 was a single, mutable production surface shared by every customer worldwide, any behavioral improvement–even changing a counter-intuitive default or modernizing an error format–carried the risk of breaking existing scripts or required multi-year migrations. With interface-based versioning (IBV) , aligned with Google AIP-185 , Compute Engine introduces immutable, date-based API snapshots alongside /v1 : Stable versions ( YYYY-MM-DD ) : Released on a predictable quarterly cadence (starting with 2026-09-01 ), each stable version represents a locked, point-in-time contract of all generally available Compute Engine features and behavioral defaults. Stable versions don't receive breaking changes after they're published. They have no end-of-support date today. Preview versions ( YYYY-MM-DD-preview ) : Released on a rapid cadence (such as 2026-10-01-preview ), preview versions branch from a stable parent to give developers early access to upcoming features and API designs, carrying a predictable one-year lifespan for testing and feedback. Uninterrupted /v1 support : The existing /v1 API remains fully supported and it continues to serve as the default if no date-based version is specified. Your existing applications, scripts, and integrations continue to work without modification. Primary benefits for builders 1. Stability and customer-controlled upgrades In a traditional single-version API, changing a default behavior forces a trade-off between platform progress and customer stability. But date-based multi-versioning puts upgrade timing entirely in your hands: Pin to a known contract : Direct REST callers and SDK users can lock onto a specific version identifier (such as 2026-09-01 ) knowing its request and response schemas are frozen. Upgrade on your schedule : When a new quarterly stable version introduces updated defaults or modified resource schemas, your team can evaluate the release notes, test in staging by changing a single version string, and roll out to production at your own pace. Consistent resource URIs : Date-based versions continue to use the /compute/v1/ base URL path. You specify the target version via the X-Goog-Api-Version HTTP header or the $apiVersion query parameter. This means that resource selfLink URIs remain uniform across tools and services. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Request a specific date-based stable version using the HTTP header
curl -X GET \
 "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/my-project/zones/us-central1-a/instances" \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
 -H "X-Goog-Api-Version: 2026-09-01"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fb5e8891650>)])]> 2. Safer defaults, stronger resilience, and modern API standards By isolating behavioral changes to new date-based versions, Compute Engine is delivering improvements that make cloud applications more resilient, more secure, and easier to automate: Resilient global queries by default : In legacy /v1 , calling AggregatedList across all zones and regions defaults returnPartialSuccess to false . This means a transient issue in a single zone could cause a global list request to fail unless callers explicitly opted in. In new date-based versions, partial success is enabled by default so global fleet queries remain resilient during localized maintenance or disruptions. Actionable, machine-readable errors (AIP-193) : Date-based versions adopt standardized google.rpc.ErrorInfo payloads with structured reason , domain , and contextual metadata (such as returning the list of supported_versions if an invalid version identifier is requested), eliminating brittle regex parsing of error strings. Stronger security and least-privilege hygiene : New API versions allow Compute Engine to tighten overly broad legacy IAM permission checks and introduce safer configuration defaults without disrupting legacy automation running on /v1 . Cleaner, declarative-friendly API design : Multi-versioning provides a clean path to evolve complex, decade-old resource schemas toward modern Google API Improvement Proposals (AIPs). 3. Seamless adoption across client libraries, gcloud , and Terraform Whether you call the REST API directly or manage infrastructure through higher-level tools, Compute Engine API Multi-Versioning is designed to work without friction: Surface How multi-versioning works Your responsibility Client libraries (Python, Go, Java, Node.js, C#, Ruby, PHP) Each SDK release automatically binds to a specific date-based API version while preserving the /v1 package namespace ( compute_v1 , apiv1 ). Enums are represented as strings for seamless forward and backward compatibility. Upgrade your client library dependency as usual– no import path rewrites required . Use -preview SDK releases to test preview features. Google Cloud CLI ( gcloud ) gcloud compute targets the bundled stable API version. The new gcloud preview compute command group targets the bundled preview API version. Keep gcloud updated. Existing gcloud compute , beta , and alpha scripts continue to work as-is. Terraform ( google & google-beta ) The google provider targets stable date-based APIs, while google-beta targets preview APIs under the hood. Upgrade your Terraform provider version to adopt new features; no manual API version configuration needed in HCL scripts. Direct HTTP / REST Select any active version via -H "X-Goog-Api-Version: YYYY-MM-DD" or ?$apiVersion=YYYY-MM-DD , and fetch version-specific Discovery Documents . Pass the header or query parameter in your HTTP client to opt into a specific version (e.g., 2026-09-01 , 2026-10-01-preview ). Get started Compute Engine API multi-versioning is available today across all Google Cloud regions, with 2026-09-01 as the initial stable version and 2026-10-01-preview available for preview testing. title: New capabilities to power agents at scale with Google's Agentic Data Cloud
raw_text: Not long ago, we were entering the agentic era; today, organizations are deriving significant value from running agents in production. The opportunity to capture new revenue streams, improve efficiency, and manage risk makes reimagining operations with agents top of mind for enterprise leaders. That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a System of Action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost. Leading organizations such as PayPal, Siemens, Telus, Vodafone, Walmart, and more are already achieving business impact with us today. Today, we’re sharing key updates to Google’s Agentic Data Cloud. We’re empowering your agents everywhere, grounding them in your enterprise context to deliver accurate, trusted answers, and providing elevated agentic-first experiences for both practitioners and business users. Activate all your data for agents with the borderless Lakehouse Enterprise data lives everywhere — across multi-cloud environments, on-premises systems, and SaaS platforms like Confluent, SAP, Salesforce, and Workday. The borderless Lakehouse , built on the open Apache Iceberg format, lets you activate all of your data, wherever it lives, so that your agents have one governed foundation. Instead of moving data, stitching together connectors, or paying surprise variable egress fees, you get a stack tuned at every layer, from the infrastructure to the model. In fact, Apache Iceberg data under management has more than tripled over the past year. Today, we are announcing several new enhancements for the borderless Lakehouse. Gemini now works directly on your borderless Lakehouse allowing business users to use natural language to query records that live across clouds while agents ground their reasoning and drive business workflows. With cross-cloud interconnect and caching for AWS and Azure , now generally available, you can query data across clouds with a private, secure connection and zero variable egress fees. And when you query remote cloud data, Lakehouse automatically caches retrieved data blocks locally within Google Cloud. Additionally, customers can use the open Iceberg catalog federation with Databricks Unity, Snowflake Horizon, and AWS Glue as well as zero-copy integrations with SAP, Workday, and Salesforce. To deliver context for AI, the borderless Lakehouse integrates directly with Knowledge Catalog , to automatically index your distributed and unstructured data, in cloud storage, giving agents the right context to be accurate, while controlling token costs for an intelligent and sustainable agentic strategy . "By implementing the borderless Lakehouse that federates single-copy Apache Iceberg data from Amazon S3 tables to BigQuery, Delivery Hero's talabat reduced data-movement costs by approximately 40% while making streaming transactional events queryable across both clouds within minutes of production." - Harish Ramesh, Staff Data Engineer, Delivery Hero talabat To take action in the moment, agents need simultaneous access to both your historical analytical data, and real-time transactional data. That’s why today we're announcing new AlloyDB integrations with the borderless Lakehouse . With direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB , you can now directly query Iceberg tables stored in cloud storage, without any ETL pipelines or copies, and join live operational data with historical lakehouse data in a single PostgreSQL query. By combining AlloyDB's transactional capabilities with direct Iceberg table access, systems can efficiently bridge transactional and analytical data to meet rigorous demands from agents. It is fully integrated with the Lakehouse runtime catalog , allowing you to register Iceberg tables in AlloyDB alongside the rest of your tables. Everything automatically shows up in Knowledge Catalog — so your agents get the same governed context. AlloyDB direct Iceberg access is up to 7x faster on aggregation queries than Amazon’s comparable PostgreSQL-compatible service. And completing this borderless strategy, Spanner Omni , which is generally available, brings Google-grade consistency, scale, and multi-model capabilities to hybrid agentic applications across on premises, edge nodes, and multi-cloud environments. Deliver accurate, trusted answers by grounding every agent in enterprise context Agents are only as accurate as the business context they are grounded in. Knowledge Catalog is Google Cloud’s universal context engine that turns raw data into shared business context for agents to answer and act with higher accuracy, trust, and token efficiency. Today, we’re taking Knowledge Catalog to the next level by extending our AI-driven context curation capabilities with self-learning, reusable context sets, and a reimagined user experience so your context layer is built and evolved automatically with your business while keeping humans in full control of their data governance. Based on our internal benchmarks, Knowledge Catalog makes AI agents nearly 4x more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens. Much of an enterprise’s institutional knowledge lives outside their databases in operational playbooks, documents, and tickets, and context for agents must be curated around the questions people actually ask. With the new self-learning enrichment in Knowledge Catalog, available in preview, agents take on the heavy lifting of context curation. Knowledge Catalog learns from user intent and every human and agent interaction by continuously mining unstructured sources like Google Workspace, GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and SharePoint to close context gaps and evolve context automatically. It also packages domain knowledge into reusable Open Knowledge Format (OKF) context sets, allowing context engineers and data stewards to govern this enriched context effortlessly. For data stewards and data teams, we also introduced, a new studio experience in Knowledge Catalog , in preview, which provides a conversational user interface where you can explore context in natural language, visualize your entire data estate across cloud environments and SaaS applications, and review, audit, and approve proposed enrichment updates with full versioning and rollback. New studio experience in Knowledge Catalog showcasing conversational context exploration and an interactive graph Additionally, we announced that Knowledge Catalog is now on by default in Gemini , in preview. Every data question is now grounded in a governed business context automatically. When you connect BigQuery, AlloyDB, Cloud SQL, or Spanner, Knowledge Catalog resolves business terms, locates trusted tables, and determines join paths before generating SQL — under each user’s own access permissions. This gives organizations the confidence to deploy agents at enterprise scale because your agents draw from shared, registered context sets for consistent accuracy, lower latency, and reduced token costs. Finally, because critical business definitions cannot be left to an LLM’s guesswork, Knowledge Catalog grounds agents in trusted semantic models , now generally available, from BigQuery, Looker (LookML), Databricks, Snowflake, dbt, and SAP, without moving data. Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on. Knowledge Catalog also extends metadata discovery and federation to Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud, Snowflake, Databricks Unity Catalog, and third-party catalogs like Atlan and Collibra — building on the catalog investments you’ve already made so your entire data estate is universally understood by every agent. Transforming practitioner experiences with agents We are reimagining how data professionals and business teams work — elevating practitioners from individual contributors supported by co-assistants, into orchestrators of autonomous agents that drive intent-driven business outcomes. For both technical teams and everyday business users, we introduced two new purpose-built capabilities in Gemini, at the recent Gemini at Work event. For Data and ML engineers, we are extending Gemini with machine learning skills and tools that back every data scientist and data engineer with a team of agents. Engineers describe the outcome they want in plain language, and Gemini generates PySpark code, provides notebooks to edit and test it, trains models, and troubleshoots and fixes pipeline issues on its own. And for business users, anyone in your organization can generate reliable, real-time operational reports simply by asking. Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query. Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent, verified answers every time. Now, for developers who'd rather stay in their own tools, we recently announced the general availability of the Data Agent Kit . It eliminates console hopping and ETL boilerplate by integrating Google Data Cloud tools directly into your developers' preferred IDEs and CLIs — like VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity. Armed with native MCP tooling, practitioners define business intent and let agents generate, tune, and test data pipelines. Engineering a data infrastructure built for agent scale As organizations scale to millions of agents collaborating across workflows, traditional database architectures break down. We’re introducing tailored infrastructure engineered specifically for agent scale. To accelerate rapid testing and prototyping, today we’re announcing AlloyDB Express , in preview. This is a new edition of AlloyDB designed for builders and coding agents who need extreme development velocity. It offers sub-2-second instant provisioning, scale-to-zero pause and resume, secure private IP connectivity, integrated observability, and a small footprint with 1–2 vCPUs and 20GB of storage. AlloyDB now provides a developer-first, PostgreSQL environment for agent development and testing. For production environments, we recently announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB , in preview, which enables thousands of collaborating AI agents to query live transactional data with complete workload isolation. With the agentic database architecture , agents achieve sub-millisecond I/O, and terabit-per-second aggregated scan throughput, supporting over 3 million queries per second. Compute scales automatically based on active reasoning sessions and scales back to zero when idle without affecting production systems. For running open-source data infrastructure, Managed Service for Apache Spark extends its price-performance advantage compared to market alternatives by over 3x through further improvements to Lightning Engine. Recent enhancements for Spark 4.0 include faster startup at no additional cost, beneficial for interactive workloads and small batch ETL jobs. In addition, the premium tier provides performance boosts by pairing upgraded hardware with software acceleration from the Lightning Engine, and this is on by default. Finally, we’ve continued to enhance BigQuery for agent scale. In the past year alone, we've made queries over 40% faster while cutting query processing cost by more than 50% through intelligent optimizations like fluid scaling and built-in workload acceleration. BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics directly on relational tables with zero ETL. It allows organizations to model data as nodes and edges to uncover complex, hidden relationships without moving data into a separate graph database. And today, two new models from Google Research run natively in BigQuery. The first is TimesFM 3.0 , now in preview, which lets you generate forecasts directly in SQL with no custom models to train or manage and TabFM , also now in preview, which brings predictive machine learning directly into BigQuery. Get started today In addition to these announcements, we continue to enhance core performance, cost management, and operational resilience across our broader data ecosystem. Ready to transform your data estate into an active System of Action? Explore our Agentic Data Cloud page, sign up for a Data Strategy Workshop and start building your agentic enterprise, at no cost, with Google Cloud. You can also head over to our Trusted Agents, Real Outcomes digital event to catch our Agentic Data Cloud vision and the latest innovations. See the portfolio in action, learn from Yahoo’s real-world blueprint, and unpack deep-dive sessions with product leaders across Databases, Data Analytics, and BI.

title: Unify operational and Lakehouse data with direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
raw_text:
To make good business decisions, you need two kinds of data: the live state of the business from operational databases, and the historical context stored in an analytical system such as a lakehouse or a data warehouse. Traditionally, those systems have been separate, but they are now converging rapidly. That’s why today, we're announcing direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL , in preview. Now, developers can query Apache Iceberg tables stored in a cloud storage bucket directly from AlloyDB and join them with live operational data, all in a single SQL query. In addition, we’re announcing the general availability of AlloyDB sync and Lakehouse federation . Together, they give AlloyDB three ways to work with the borderless Lakehouse, which keeps one open copy of your data available to any engine. Etsy , for example, unified three petabytes with the borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%. With AlloyDB, which approach to use depends on where the data lives and how your application reads it: Direct Iceberg access: Read Iceberg tables in place, accelerated by the AlloyDB columnar engine. AlloyDB sync: Serve lakehouse data from AlloyDB for your most latency-sensitive workloads, refreshed on a schedule you set. Lakehouse federation: Query native BigQuery tables in place, with BigQuery doing the processing. With this launch, apps and agents can act on operational and lakehouse data together without building or managing custom pipelines. AlloyDB and the borderless Lakehouse: Query Apache Iceberg and BigQuery data in place or sync it to AlloyDB, giving real-time applications and AI agents governed access to operational and lakehouse data together. Decisions at the moment of action With these integrations between AlloyDB and the borderless Lakehouse, historical context sits next to live transactions, so decisions can happen at the moment of action, without building or managing custom pipelines. For example: Fraud and risk: Before approving a payment, a fraud agent checks it against five years of customer transaction history in Iceberg, in addition to the last 30 days in the database. Personalization: A shopping agent joins the live cart with lifetime value and return history in the lakehouse to choose the right offer while the shopper is still on the page. Dynamic pricing: A pricing agent combines live inventory in AlloyDB with years of demand and weather history in the lakehouse to adjust prices as conditions change. Data products: A data team publishes curated tables once to Iceberg, and then dozens of applications read them in place instead of each maintaining its own copy. In each case, the history stays in the lakehouse and the decision happens in the database. Agents act on your behalf using only the tables and permissions you grant them in AlloyDB. Let’s take a deeper look at each of the three integrations. Direct Iceberg access in AlloyDB (Preview) With direct Iceberg access, AlloyDB reads Apache Iceberg tables directly from Cloud Storage, using either a bucket path or the Lakehouse runtime catalog. You register an Iceberg table once and query it like any other PostgreSQL table, including joins with live operational tables. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Register five years of transaction history stored as Iceberg
CREATE TABLE transaction_history (
 customer_id BIGINT, category TEXT, amount NUMERIC, ts TIMESTAMPTZ)
USING iceberg
WITH (uri = 'gs://my-bucket/warehouse/payments/transaction_history');


-- Compare the payment in flight with the customer's history
SELECT t.amount,
 AVG(h.amount) AS usual_spend,
 MAX(h.amount) AS largest_past_purchase
FROM recent_transactions t -- live, in AlloyDB
JOIN transaction_history h -- five years, in Iceberg
 ON h.customer_id = t.customer_id AND h.category = t.category
WHERE t.transaction_id = 'TX-1001'
GROUP BY t.amount;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fb5e8893a50>)])]> AlloyDB reads Iceberg tables in place and joins them with live operational data, using the same copy as the rest of your lakehouse. Iceberg support is built into AlloyDB and is accelerated by the AlloyDB columnar engine , so queries over lakehouse data are fast. They run on the same database instance as your application, without a separate reader instance to manage, and they read the latest data your team has published to the lakehouse. In our testing on a 1 TB dataset in Cloud Storage, AlloyDB direct Iceberg access is up to 7x faster on aggregation queries than Amazon's comparable PostgreSQL-compatible service, and up to 3.5x faster on aggregation queries than the open-source PostgreSQL extension. AlloyDB sync for the lowest-latency reads (GA) Not every table needs to be read in place. A retail merchant risk score, for example, is checked before every payment but only changes when the data team recomputes it overnight. Data like this, read on every request and refreshed on a schedule, is fastest as a local table in AlloyDB. The challenge is keeping that copy fresh without building and maintaining a pipeline. AlloyDB sync copies lakehouse data from BigQuery into AlloyDB, once or on a schedule, and keeps it refreshed. The copy is a local AlloyDB table, so your app reads it as fast as any other table, and you can index it, serve it from read pools, or use it with the columnar engine and vector search. You can start a sync with one click from the BigQuery console or from SQL: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Keep merchant risk scores refreshed every hour
SELECT alloydb_sync.create_bq_sync_table(

 INTERVAL '1 hour');"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fb5e8a02b50>)])]> Lakehouse federation (GA) For organizations with years of analytical history already in BigQuery, Lakehouse federation lets AlloyDB query native BigQuery tables in place and join them with live operational data in a single query. AlloyDB pushes filters, aggregations, and limits down to BigQuery, which does most of the processing and sends back only the results. You can also set which project is billed for these queries and restrict which roles can use them. Google Cloud customers like Loyal Guru are already pairing AlloyDB and BigQuery in this way. "AlloyDB, along with other Google Cloud products like BigQuery, provides the agility and performance needed to continually enhance our platform's capabilities and help us anticipate emerging trends rather than merely reacting." - Javi Fernández, Co-founder & CTO, Loyal Guru Choose the right approach and get started The convergence of operational and analytical systems is underway; how you choose to approach it in a Google Cloud environment depends on your use case: Direct Iceberg access: Best for historical data in Iceberg that your app joins with live data, accelerated by the AlloyDB columnar engine. Try it: Enable direct Iceberg access on a PostgreSQL 18 instance and follow: Access Iceberg data from AlloyDB . AlloyDB sync: Best for tables your app reads constantly and needs at the lowest latency. The copy is as fresh as its last refresh. Build: Pick a table in BigQuery and choose to sync to AlloyDB using the Google Cloud console or psql. title: How Nammu21 automates syndicated loans on Google Cloud Universal Ledger
raw_text: The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction. To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements and instantiate them as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL) , Nammu21 automates the entire loan lifecycle, paving the way for improved settlement times and greater market efficiency. Digitizing the loan market While loan markets provide billions in capital to businesses worldwide, their underlying infrastructure has not kept pace with the speed of digital finance. This landscape requires continuous coordination across facility agents, borrowers, and diverse lender syndicates, while also managing highly customized credit agreements with dynamic tranches and complex covenants. In particular, relying on fragmented, manual interpretation of legal text often results in significant operational drag and data silos. According to the Loan Market Association , secondary market settlement times for par/near par loans in Q4 2024 still averaged 42 days, with a median of 27 days. These notoriously slow timelines tie up capital, increase counterparty risk, and create a heavy reconciliation burden for participants. Nammu21 transforms bespoke credit documents into programmable assets at scale by rendering each facility's governing terms as a Digital Credit Instrument (DCI). The DCI maps every term — including conditions, consents, eligibility criteria, and operational mechanics that determine what is permitted under a facility — directly back to its originating legal provision. These elements are then expressed as executable behaviours against a loan's live state. To instantiate these instruments, the proof-of-concept utilizes the secure, high-performance execution environment of GCUL, an institutional-grade, permissioned distributed ledger that helps automate complex financial workflows to deliver near-instant transaction finality and predictable costs without the volatility or security concerns of public blockchains. A purpose-built stack for digital credit Combined with Nammu21’s data intelligence, GCUL provides the foundational infrastructure for converting legal document logic into live, programmable contracts. Designed to handle the privacy, scale, and multi-party coordination required by institutional finance, GCUL provides a permissioned, high-performance distributed ledger that delivers deterministic, instant transaction finality for high-value financial settlements. Programmable contracts on GCUL are written in gculpy , GCUL's domain-optimized programming language. As a strict, statically-typed subset of Python, gculpy is designed to be safe, readable, and auditable, making it ideal for processing complex financial logic. For regulated financial institutions, gculpy offers distinct operational advantages over other ledger programming models. The language simplifies development by removing the need for complex memory management or workarounds to meet highly restrictive call stack limits, allowing engineers to focus on the financial logic itself. GCUL also provides robust, built-in permissioning, requiring explicit user authorization before a contract can store data on their behalf. This solves the "unsolicited asset" problem — common on public networks — where unwanted tokens can be sent to an organization's wallet, creating compliance and accounting issues. With GCUL, institutions can maintain full control over which assets they interact with to support their high-value, highly regulated use cases. Nammu21 serves a dual role in this architecture. First, the platform renders the DCI programmatically from the original legal agreement without manual document reading to establish the terms. Next, it derives gculpy contracts that define the structure of the obligation and govern the loan on GCUL, using the DCI to supply the terms that determine what the loan documents permit, require and block. Technical architecture: The loan lifecycle on GCUL Nammu21’s loan implementation on GCUL demonstrates the value of creating a single, immutable source of truth. The proof-of-concept modeled a $1.945 billion Term Loan B — one segment of a broader multi-facility transaction — where the agent bank, borrower, transferor, and transferee all worked off a permissioned view of the same on-ledger rendering. The lifecycle begins when an agent bank selects a specific credit agreement transformed by Nammu21. The platform instantly provides the structured terms from the document, which are used to instantiate a unique gculpy contract on GCUL, establishing a verifiable, on-ledger digital twin of that specific loan facility. Next, the agent bank initiates the onboarding of the borrower and lenders. This multilateral action requires that each participant review the request and then provide explicit consent by approving the onboarding invitation from their own interface. Once all parties are onboarded, the agent bank records an immutable hash of the loan's key terms on-ledger, attesting that the on-ledger data matches the canonical off-ledger records. Subsequent lifecycle events, such as secondary market transfers or repayments, are also managed as multi-step, automated workflows governed by a consent-driven model. For example, a transfer of a loan position requires new lender, borrower, and agent bank consent before it can be executed atomically on the ledger. All payment flows, from interest payments to loan close-outs, settle directly on GCUL using tokenized commercial bank money, eliminating the need for external payment rails. Transacting with familiar, regulated money on a programmable ledger provides an architecture purpose-built for institutional finance, grounded in three core pillars: 1. Compliance via gated execution: Nammu21’s gculpy contracts instantiated with governing terms, validate every action against the terms transformed from the agreement before execution, mitigating potential covenant breaches or invalid transfers upfront while eliminating the risk of silent failures. 2. Role-based privacy: GCUL enforces strict, role-based access, ensuring that trading strategies, positions, and sensitive loan data remain confidential and are visible only to the necessary counterparties in a transaction. 3. Settlement finality: Every on-ledger action completes near-instantly and anchors on canonical data derived from the original credit agreement, replacing provisional, reconciliation-heavy models with real-time, trusted verification. The business impact of moving on-ledger This proof-of-concept illustrates a structural shift in how credit markets can operate. When each facility's governing terms are rendered as a DCI and executed on GCUL, the operational mechanics of lending markets change fundamentally, rather than incrementally. Values can be reconciled bilaterally, but governance logic cannot – and the market’s current friction stems directly from each party's independent interpretation of the rules. Resolving this issue on-ledger is what enables settlement times to compress, back-office overhead to shrink, and counterparty risk to be mitigated by design rather than by manual checking. This same architecture can be applied wherever credit terms are bespoke and manually interpreted. By freeing up capital that would otherwise be trapped in lengthy settlement cycles, new liquidity is unlocked and a more dynamic and efficient secondary loan market can emerge. title: Leading in the agentic era: How to put people first as you adopt AI agents
raw_text: Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations. In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish. While budget, compute, and tooling can help launch an agent program, enterprise adoption takes intentional culture work. People need to feel empowered enough to experiment with agents, and leaders need to show teams what agents mean for their roles. Based on our work across these organizations, we’ve put together five practical lessons for guiding enterprises through an agentic shift. 1. Make workflows agent-executed, human-directed Most enterprise workflows run like a relay race: one person completes a task, checks it, and hands it off to the next person, who then does the same. Layering an AI agent onto that model gives you a faster runner for one leg, but the handoffs may stall or slow down other work. Redesigning your workflows can remove blockers like these in a few ways: Strategic direction: Move from human-in-the-loop validation (where a person checks each step) to a human-in-the- lead model. Agents take on the work, and people set the direction and own the outcomes. Parallel dependencies: One agent can handle every dependency at once instead of passing work through a multi-person queue. For example, an agent can check product availability, credit limits, and contract paperwork at the same time without waiting on each step to finish. Manage by exception: Once the process is set up this way, the agent absorbs routine deterministic transactions, routing only ambiguous or high-judgment scenarios to human review. Cross-team stalls disappear, and your team stays in control. 2. Turn hesitation into ownership In our experience, the biggest barrier to adoption is trust. Many employees worry about their value if an agent handles most of their day-to-day tasks. Others are concerned with who takes the blame if an agent makes a mistake. We encourage teams to treat agents the way they'd treat a junior team member: Active delegation: Frame agents as digital coworkers. That means assigning tasks to them, defining their scope, and checking their work for accuracy. Clear responsibilities: Set boundaries around which decisions an agent can make and which require human sign-off. When team members know exactly where accountability sits, they can better direct agents. Comfort through exposure : Confidence grows through familiarity. We recommend starting with low-stakes use cases (like scheduling internal meetings) to help motivate teams before moving to high-stakes operations (such as financial forecasting). 3. Manage hybrid teams of people and agents Next, it’s important to support collaboration when you bring agents into your team. Let’s look at how this might work in practice, Focus on results: Collaborate across teams to break down workflows at both the tool and task level. Cross-functional perspectives reveal an end-to-end view of the process, helping you pinpoint where agentic capabilities belong and how to prioritize ideas by technical feasibility and business impact. Reinforce behaviors: Top performers on a hybrid team are the people who guide their agents well. Reward team members for auditing an agent's reasoning and catching when its logic drifts from company goals. Coach your teams: Show your teams how to work with agents so people can spend more time on creative work and decision-making. 4. Build agentic literacy through experimentation Your teams need to understand how agents solve problems. People who know where an agent's logic breaks down (and why) can guide and judge its output. Beyond the tool: Literacy covers both writing a good prompt and auditing the result. Agents choose the most likely path instead of following deterministic rules, so people need to know when to trust an agent's output and when to check it. Safe learning zones: Give business roles the same sandbox access that technical teams get to build agentic literacy across the whole organization. Celebrating intelligent failure: Experimentation is how teams learn. In our experience, we’ve seen that when teams build an agent that fails because the data wasn't accurate, that team then understands how important data readiness is. Even if it didn’t work out, this should still be encouraged so your teams keep experimenting. 5. Govern agents with a hub-and-spoke model To roll agents out across an enterprise, you need central guardrails that don't slow down the teams closest to the work. A hub-and-spoke model does both: it gives teams a shared foundation to build on and room to move at their own pace. The hub: Establish a central AI council team that sets guidelines, maintains ethical guardrails, and manages a library of approved tools. That way, teams don't rebuild the same things. The spokes: Allow individual teams to adapt those tools to their own needs, experiment quickly, and give feedback on what works in practice. Within Google Cloud Consulting, we use our internal Agent Catalog to share low-code agents and skills that drive cross-team learning, innovation, and efficiency. However, you don’t need to build a custom platform to implement this. Here are a few approaches: Filter and sort agents made by employees through a simple internal web app. Publish and share agents with built-in Gemini Enterprise features like Agent Gallery. Work directly with technical teams that help organizations create tailored solutions. Lead with a people-first approach to AI Becoming an agentic organization is about your people. Give your teams systems and guardrails to move fast, room to experiment, and leadership that promotes accountability. Ultimately, the overarching goal is to build an organization where human ingenuity and agents support and amplify one another. Join a Build with Gemini workshop : Sign up today to discover hands-on strategies for creating agentic literacy and empowering your teams to lead with AI.

title: Debian, Ubuntu patch APT flaw that could hand attackers root
raw_text: Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives, that could allow attackers to install unverified software with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-109518 , the vulnerability could let an attacker positioned to manipulate HTTP traffic between an APT client and an archive server install an attacker-controlled package without verification. Debian disclosed the flaw on November 4, crediting security researcher Max Justicz. Ubuntu subsequently rated it High, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.7. “I used an AI for two hours and found a zero-day that would let a nation-state hack any server running stock Ubuntu,” Justicz said in an X post . Successful exploitation could allow arbitrary code execution with root privileges on a vulnerable machine. Both distributions have issued fixes. Redirects and retries turn hardlinks into an attack surface The problem lies in APT’s handling of HTTP redirects and resumed downloads. “APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives them the same URI,” Debian’s advisory said. “Improper file handling when resuming an HTTP download allows a man-in-the-middle ( MitM ) attacker to replace a package after verification, resulting in the execution of arbitrary code as root.” APT developers provide a more detailed explanation: an attacker can exploit redirects and transient HTTP server errors that trigger download retries, causing APT to override existing hard links with a chosen payload. Because Debian packages are installed with root privileges, successfully substituting a package can lead to arbitrary code execution as root. Ubuntu described the required attack position as an on-path attacker able to manipulate traffic between the package client and the archive server. A malicious mirror or proxy could provide that position, but the attack requires specific download conditions. Retry settings decide who is exposed The vulnerability depends on APT’s Acquire::Retries setting being non-zero. APT developers say this has been the default since version 2.3.2, although scripts may have enabled retries on older installations. Ubuntu specifies that the default retry value of three applies from Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) onward. Older releases are not exposed by default, but may still be vulnerable if retries have been enabled. Debian 13 (Trixie) is patched in APT 3.0.4, while Debian 12 (Bookworm) received the fix in version 2.6.2. Ubuntu has also released patched packages for supported releases, including 22.04 LTS, 24.04.LTS, and 26.04 LTS. Ubuntu 26.10 was also affected, with its fix being published when Ubuntu’s November 4 advisory appeared. The fix addresses the underlying file-handling issue. In a commit authored on October 12, APT developer Julian Andres Klode changed the download code to open destination files exclusively, unlinking existing files before copying over any partially downloaded content. The change prevents downloads from writing through existing hard links, which could otherwise redirect writes to unintended files. Ubuntu recommends updating APT and temporarily disabling retries during remediation. It also advises using HTTPS for package downloads, which protects against traffic manipulation in this attack scenario. For enterprise security teams, the priority is to identify vulnerable installations, check retry configurations, and ensure patched packages reach production systems and the Linux images used to provision them.

title: Zyxel patches a zero-day hiding behind an old fix
raw_text: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed. The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 , is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0. Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September. However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29. The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.
