title: Building incident playbooks for machine identity breaches
raw_text: Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with. Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. The same goes for an API key buried in a build pipeline, or an OAuth token somebody granted to a SaaS integration back in 2022 and hasn’t thought about since. Once one of those is stolen, your analysts are running a script that was written with people in mind, and the cracks tend to show well before the first shift handover. There are also far more of them than most boards realise. CyberArk’s research puts machine identities at roughly 82 for every human identity . Very few sit behind MFA, and a fair number hold far more access than the job they were built for. I’d add a problem that gets less airtime, which is that their traffic lives in the background noise your monitoring was tuned to filter out. Where the human playbook stalls Ownership is usually the first thing to slow you down. When a person’s account is compromised, HR can tell you who they are and who their manager is before you’ve finished your coffee. A service account pulling data it shouldn’t comes with no such shortcut, so the analyst burns the first hour working out which team built it. More often than anyone likes to admit, that trail ends at a contractor who left the business a year earlier. Say you do find an owner; containment still isn’t the clean step it is for a person. Lock a user out and one employee loses an afternoon. Pull a credential that a payments integration depends on, though, and you might take a customer-facing service down, which no analyst wants on their name at 11 p.m. without sign-off. So, they go hunting for somebody senior enough to approve the outage while the attacker carries on. Detection is the part people underestimate. An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours. Your impossible-travel rules were built around people moving between cities, so they have nothing to compare against here. Figure 1: One alert split into two paths. Ashish Mishra What recent breaches show Cloudflare’s write-up of its Thanksgiving 2023 security incident is worth a quarter of an hour of any CISO’s time. The attackers came in with one access token and three service account credentials lifted during the earlier Okta support breach. Cloudflare had rotated thousands of credentials after Okta, yet missed those four because the team believed, wrongly, that nothing was using them. The alert that finally fired came more than a week after the attackers first logged in, when they added one of those service accounts to an administrator group. Microsoft’s case turned on a test application nobody had cleaned up. Its guidance for responders on the Midnight Blizzard attack describes a password spray against a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. Inside that tenant sat an old test OAuth app that still held elevated access to the corporate environment, and the attackers used it to get into corporate email accounts. Drift is the case I’d put in front of a board. In August 2025, attackers got hold of the OAuth tokens that Salesloft’s Drift chatbot used to talk to Salesforce, and for roughly ten days they pulled records out of one customer’s Salesforce instance after another. Google’s threat intelligence team, which tracked the campaign closely , concluded the attackers were mostly after credentials. Once the data was out, they went digging through it for AWS access keys and passwords, anything that might get them into the next company along. I don’t think any of the three needed a clever attacker at the front door. In each case, a credential was issued for a piece of work and then left alone long after the work had finished. Getting the groundwork in first It is a relatively simple task to create a playbook. However, a playbook relies upon an inventory. In many organizations, this inventory consists of a service account list generated from Active Directory where half of the description fields have been left blank. Each time you identify a high-privilege non-human identity, document the team responsible for that identity, and provide a brief explanation (one or two sentences) describing what will fail should you remove that identity. Many people do not include the explanation as to why something would fail if removed, since obtaining this information requires contacting the application team for clarification; this contact would otherwise be initiated by your analyst at 3:00 AM while the attacker remains active within your network. Next, sort those identities by blast radius. I wouldn’t put a read-only reporting token on the same response path as a cloud admin service principal, and I doubt your auditors would either. For the top tier, settle in advance who’s allowed to authorise an immediate revoke even if it knocks something over, and put that role in the playbook by name. Executives must own that call. If you leave it with whoever’s on shift, you’ll get a polite wait for permission while the token stays live. For SOCI-regulated entities, there’s an extra edge to this, because the 12-hour window for reporting a significant cyber incident to ASD can be running while that conversation drags on. Triage that fits a machine No one can provide a response to “was this you?”, thus, replace it with questions that can be answered by the log files. A rapid means of verification is location: where do the credentials usually sign in from, and where are they signing in from at present? Logging is readily available via Cloud Audit Logs and Workload Identity Platforms, if someone turned the logging on. Permissions take longer but tell you more. Line up what the identity holds against what it has used over the last few months, because attackers tend to go straight for high-risk scopes that have been sitting idle. I’d give persistence the same attention. With a privileged service principal in hand, an attacker will often mint new secrets or register an app of their own, and none of that goes away when you revoke the original credential. Containment without breaking the business The “trigger” for rotation and revocation should be written separately in the playbook. Rotation would be appropriate when you are reasonably confident that the attacker has not escalated and the organization cannot afford to lose the integration. Revocation is the obvious choice if you find evidence of an ongoing attack; this will be clear enough so there will be no debate at midnight. Pre-staging your replacement credentials will make revocations tolerable. When the team that owns the application has previously tested how to generate a new credential and then store it in their secret management system, revoking old credentials can cost you about ten minutes of downtime instead of being a full-day disruption. Ask the team to practice generating and storing new credentials during a low-traffic week. Do not find out mid-incident that the runbook references a vault location that was renamed last year. Scoping and recovery To understand the full scope of an incident, look at the entire lifespan of the machine credential, not just the period after the alert was generated. Because machines may be able to go undetected as being compromised for many months prior to discovery, the first unusual activity reported will most likely not be the first unusual activity performed. Also, keep in mind that “drift” is a great way to remember to see what information the identity has access to, and if anyone has placed credentials into that identity. If so, each addition of a secret will require you to add a new rotation to your list. Recovery is when you fix what caused the problem in the first place. For example, if a static secret was compromised, determine if that workload can use short-lived tokens using Workload Identity Federation; or perhaps a short-lived token can be generated on demand (Just-In-Time) and will expire automatically. Recovery is a tedious, non-sexy task, and most of the time it requires financial support from an entity outside of the Security Operations Center (SOC). Before finalizing the playbook, conduct a tabletop simulation with the application owners in attendance along with the Security Operations Center (SOC). Select your highest-privilege integration and simulate a stolen-token event (from first alert through recovery). During the simulation, when a decision needs to be made regarding who approves revoking the token, and revoking the token will disrupt production, observe how much time it takes for the team to identify who should make this approval.

Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments. Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity. The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies. By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden. For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations. Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic , the free community version. Read the Adaptive Detonation blog post for technical details, malware case studies, and original and follow-up analysis reports. title: Attackers turned OpsShield’s trusted update channel into a supply-chain attack
raw_text: The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process. This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers. The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys. Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves. “The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian , a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.” The anatomy of the attack OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers. The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update. The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers. About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords. OpsShield says it is still reviewing the exact request that provided access, and has patched two possible entry points and verified related vendor components “line by line.” It closed the attacker’s account, revoked the stolen update-storage key as well as “every cloud API token and access key on our account.” The company also removed the attacker’s secure shell (SSH); deleted the clones of its servers created by the attacker plus any snapshots; turned on stronger login protection and replaced every SSH key and password; reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated all keys; and began rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers with tighter PHP and firewall settings. The company has also published clean updates: v5.88.26, which removes the hidden root shell; plus a follow-up which removes the scheduled task left by the attacker. Further, it began re-issuing all cPGuard license private and public keys so that the copies the attacker gained access to stopped working. The company advised admins to: Update cPGuard to the latest version, then confirm that /etc/cron.d/i93677 , /var/tmp/.i93677/ and /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh are gone; delete them if not; Change root passwords and every local user password on the server; Generate new root SSH keys and remove old ones from every server that trusted them; until the keys are changed, treat the servers as compromised; Change MySQL root passwords and any database passwords and rotate any password, API key, or token existing in root shell histories; Reset the OpsShield billing portal passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. Finally, it said, “if we told you the attacker logged in to your server by hand, rebuild it from a clean backup taken before 1 November.” OpsShield being transparent, but the impacts are still real “Frankly, few vendors write a breach disclosure this candid,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “OpsShield deserves a lot of credit for that.” However, he pointed out, the worst kind of breach is the one a security tool delivers. Update channels are left unlocked on purpose, and security tools run as root because they have to see everything, “so the fake update ran as root too.” For a hosting provider, one server can hold hundreds of customer websites and databases. A MySQL root password opens all of them, and a root SSH key grants access to every other server that trusts it. Shell history also often contains typed passwords and tokens. The downstream customer may be hit hardest while knowing the least, Dickson pointed out, as most website owners have no idea which security agent their hosting provider runs. Every server that updates itself trusts the vendor’s pipeline. OpsShield describes itself as a small team selling to smaller hosts at a low price, which is the uncomfortable truth of the supply chain, Dickson said. “Your exposure is set by the smallest vendor holding root on your servers, not the largest.” Avakian agreed that this serves as a reminder that an enterprise’s software supply chain is only as secure as the systems, identities, and processes behind it. “You can do everything you can to secure your own infrastructure and still get compromised through a third-party supplier you trust.” What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution mechanism to turn the vendor’s own trusted infrastructure against its customers, he noted. Third parties extend risk, which is a fact that organizations still underestimate, he said. “Enterprises need to pay much more attention to third-party and supply chain risk management.” Zero-trust a must-have Avakian also pointed out that the impact on downstream customers could go well beyond initial compromise, as stolen credentials can be used to carry out further attacks. Enterprises should take a zero-trust approach that includes their software suppliers and the updates they rely on. “Just because an update comes from a trusted source doesn’t mean you can assume it’s safe,” he said. Enterprises should take a closer look at vendor risk, protect privileged credentials, and examine software integrity. Also, continuously monitor for unexpected behavior after an update and be ready to isolate systems quickly if and when something goes wrong. “You have to plan for the possibility that even a trusted supplier can be compromised,” he emphasized. “And you need to practice those types of scenarios as part of a regular table-top exercise program.” Dickson advised starting with an inventory, and knowing every vendor agent running with root or administrator privilege, as each one is an update channel. Customers should ask vendors where update publishing keys live and what separates them from customer-facing systems, watch outbound traffic from servers, keep secrets out of shell history, and treat SSH keys as credentials with an expiration date. Downstream customers should ask their host directly whether it runs cPGuard, then change their own passwords. “The most dangerous software on your server may be the software you trust to update itself,” he said. “Choose those vendors as if they hold root, because they do.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .

title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
raw_text: Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent. The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post. The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly. “Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said , adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign. Fake installers used for real money The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software , games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads. The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software. Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session. The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates. Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing. A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization. Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators , unofficial game installers, and activation tools. Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction ( ASR ) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear. Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations. Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said. Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post. title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch to shut down rogue agents
raw_text: With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to cut off and disable models when they go rogue . Integrated into its Falcon Guardian platform, this AI Kill Switch will provide security teams with the human control to terminate the agent at its root, where it runs, block it from launching again, and even cut off its enterprise network access. The launch comes as enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents that can access sensitive data and execute tasks with limited human oversight. “These agents can access sensitive data, execute commands and interact with business applications independently, meaning enterprises may become aware of harmful incidents only after they occur. Existing security tools protect endpoints, networks and identities but may not fully understand an agent’s instructions, reasoning, tool calls and subsequent actions,” said Soumen Mandal, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research. Inside CrowdStrike’s AI kill switch The AI Kill Switch has been built on Falcon Guardian, which has the capability to discover the AI agents running in the enterprise. It uses the Falcon sensor to track what an agent is instructed to do, what it communicates, and what it executes. First, the Falcon sensor can terminate the running agent at the gateway, ensuring the malicious or misbehaving agent does not keep running while teams investigate. CrowdStrike said endpoint termination is also planned and will be available soon. Next, using the Falcon Guardian policies, the kill switch will prevent the agent from launching again on the targeted host or group of hosts. Next, it will cut-off agent’s enterprise network access. The action can be initiated by an authorised administrator, with every action being recorded in an audit trail. “Solutions such as CrowdStrike’s AI Kill Switch give enterprises a way to intervene quickly when AI agents behave unexpectedly, are compromised, or are manipulated through malicious instructions or scripts. This provides an important safeguard, allowing organisations to contain potentially dangerous or unauthorised agent activity before it causes significant damage,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and co-founder at Primus Partners. However, a kill switch should be viewed as an emergency brake, not a rewind button, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner. She added that it may prevent additional actions, but it might not necessarily reverse all the data that has already been accessed, every system that has already been changed, all communications that have already been sent, or transactions that have already been initiated. Its effectiveness will also depend on how quickly abnormal behavior is detected, which environments are covered, and whether the agent or security infrastructure has been compromised. An emergency brake, not a cure for AI risk An AI Kill Switch looks promising from the details provided, but its actual effectiveness will come in after it is used extensively in live systems, warn analysts. Also, it may be a good starting point, but it cannot be viewed as a standalone solution to enterprise AI security. “CISOs would need a more integrated approach that brings together AI discovery tools to identify unauthorised agents, runtime monitoring to track agent behaviour, robust identity and access management, and incident response and recovery mechanisms,” added Dhar. He noted that equally important is the need for stringent AI security testing and clearly defined policies governing what agents can access and execute. There should be no ambiguity around permissions, access controls or the boundaries within which these agents are allowed to operate. The objective should be to ensure that security controls are built into the entire AI agent lifecycle rather than relying on a kill switch to intervene after something goes wrong. Dhar added that enterprise AI agents often have access to sensitive systems, databases, applications, credentials, and APIs. A compromised or misdirected agent could therefore become a point of vulnerability. The challenge is compounded by the fact that such activity may go undetected for some time, making it difficult for organisations to identify and contain the threat.

title: CrowdStrike to acquire Fiddler, Dreadnode to extend AI security across agent lifecycle
raw_text: CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications. CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production. The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements. CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company. CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability “With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement. It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents. The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations. Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. CrowdStrike said the technology is intended to address risks that can arise even when agents have not been compromised. “An agent can hold valid credentials and approved tools and still make unsupported decisions, ignore instructions, or claim work it never completed. They don’t have to be compromised to create risk,” the company said in a statement. CrowdStrike plans to offer Fiddler’s technology through Falcon Observe. The product will evaluate agent accuracy, task completion, and policy compliance before deployment, and trace decisions, reasoning paths, and tool calls once agents are in production, the company said. The company further added that Falcon Observe will also detect behavioural drift, hallucinations and unintended actions, while maintaining records of agent activity for compliance and audit purposes. The offering is expected to support OpenTelemetry and frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands and Google ADK, it added. Governance remains a shared responsibility The addition of observability and automated testing to a security platform could help enterprises correlate agent behaviour with identity, runtime activity and security events, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner. However, Kaushik said the acquisitions would not make security teams the sole owners of AI agent governance. Platform and observability teams would continue to be responsible for reliability, performance and operational telemetry, while application security and AI teams would retain responsibility for secure development and testing. “Business, data and compliance leaders also retain accountability for use cases, data and regulatory obligations,” Kaushik said. She said CIOs should establish a governance model that defines responsibilities across engineering, security, risk, and business teams. CISOs, meanwhile, should ensure security teams have the authority to set minimum controls, monitor agent behaviour and intervene when activity creates unacceptable risk. Integration and roadmap questions CrowdStrike expects both transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, and has scheduled both offerings for general availability in the same quarter. Kaushik cautioned enterprises against treating the announced timelines as confirmation of final product capabilities or integration plans. “Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the pace of change of the threat landscape and evolution of AI,” she added. She advised customers to seek clarity on pricing, packaging, migration terms, service continuity, support commitments, deployment models, data handling, telemetry retention and API access. “Once the Existing and prospective customers have further details, they should set up their roadmap changes, support commitments, service continuity, contract and pricing, data portability, open integrations, and access to historical data changes,” she pointed out. CrowdStrike did not disclose the financial terms of either acquisition.

CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production. The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment.

title: CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
raw_text: “The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given. For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced. “I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.” Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure. Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028. “As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner. Taking up the agent challenge For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. In 2023, with its “Raptor” release, Falcon and the company’s flagship event took a hard turn toward AI . In this changed world, AI wasn’t simply a Falcon capability; increasingly it was Falcon, influencing everything it did. The AI theme dominated Falcon’s 2026 Fall release , bringing the company’s growing portfolio of AI SOC capabilities under the Falcon umbrella with the launch of the Agentic Security Platform. Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s Agentic Security Workforce plan but a closer look reveals important new features. Currently, agents investigate alerts using pre-built Falcon agents or custom agents built using the no-code AgentWorks solution. Charlotte AI now gives these agents a shared memory layer in Enterprise Graph that enables them to coordinate with one another across multiple endpoints, identities, and cloud services simultaneously (aided by the company’s 2025 acquisition of Onum , which accelerated the speed with which agents can ingest data). On paper, the effect is to dramatically speed up alert triage while expanding the scope and capacity of worker agents in a way that relieves human SOC teams of a lot of basic grunt work, including some Level 2 investigation and Level 3 remediation and hunting workflows. Also new is SafeMind , a frontier red-teaming system based on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-weight LLM, comprising offense (Red Tempest) and defense (Blue Solano). This agentic framework continuously tests an isolated mirror of the live environment for weaknesses, feeding the results back into detection at the agent level. CrowdStrike didn’t invent the concept, but it does appear to be the first to integrate an autonomous testing model into a SOC platform. Speed is not enough This might look brand new, but the early incarnations of the agent-powered SOC are as much evolution as revolution. Everything inside a traditional CrowdStrike-powered SOC — from its Falcon EDR sensor, Enterprise Graph data, and cloud-native management — remains in place. Humans are still essential to decision-making, albeit at a higher level than before. What agents add to this SOC paradigm is a new abstraction layer separating SOC teams from the mass of telemetry they have increasingly struggled with. This should be good news for defenders because it means they have some hope of matching the speed and scale of agentic attacks. But speed is only the beginning, points out James Patrick, CTO for the FIOR Group, which develops an AI policy and security gateway. “Attackers and defenders can both operate at machine speed, so simply making SOCs faster isn’t enough. We need to move beyond reactive detection towards continuous testing of our defenses.” SOCs must work out how much they delegate to agents and what constraints are set around this. “Enterprises already struggle with fragmented telemetry, overlapping security products and inconsistent policies. Adding autonomous systems introduces another problem: establishing who or what has authority to act, and how to verify that authority,” says Patrick. According to Chris Cochran, field CISO and VP of AI security for the SANS Institute, that’s why “for most organizations, agentic AI will be augmentative rather than a replacement for analysts, at least for the next few years.” Agent platforms, including CrowdStrike’s, still have work to do proving themselves in terms of oversight and governance. “The core problem is that we’re applying a probabilistic technology to a discipline that usually requires determinism,” Cochran adds. “A SOC needs to know that the same input will produce the same action, and that the action can be explained to an auditor or an incident review board.” For that reason, Cochran believes that while agentic-powered SOCs will remove a huge amount of alert handling and correlation effort, the workload will shift to processes such as verification. “Teams should continuously evaluate agents against known-good and known-bad cases, the same way you’d regression test detection content,” he says. “None of this is exotic, but it takes engineering time that many SOCs haven’t budgeted for.” Enemy within One deeply unfamiliar problem is that agents themselves are an emerging attack surface within the enterprise and must be constantly assessed. Traditionally, security tools defend the environment, and the idea that an agent system doing the same job could itself become a direct threat is new. But what makes agentic AI unsettlingly is its non-deterministic nature, which means that, unlike a traditional security tool, it has the potential to do things you didn’t tell it to and haven’t planned for. “Organizations are deploying autonomous systems that access sensitive data, use privileged identities, interact with applications, and execute actions. Those agents can be compromised, manipulated, or behave unexpectedly,” says Tom Findling, CEO and cofounder at AI SOC startup Conifers.ai. “Security operations will need visibility into agent identities, permissions, actions, and decision-making processes, and the ability to detect and contain dangerous behavior.” CrowdStrike’s answer, relaunched at this year’s Fal.Con, is Falcon Guardian, an AI detection and response (AIDR) solution featuring runtime enforcement, agent discovery, execution graph mapping prompts, and quarantining for misbehaving agents. Similar capabilities will be needed for any agent platform but the mere fact that security systems now need their own security systems underscores what CrowdStrike’s Sentonas was referring to with his software-as-actor remark at Fal.Con. Human SOCs need to protect their enterprises from their AI SOC helpers. To that end, CrowdStrike yesterday announced the roughly $400 million acquisition of Fiddler AI , an AI agent monitoring and governance vendor from the emerging, burgeoning, and somewhat confusing agentic AI tools ecosystem . Fiddler’s platform tracks AI models’ behavior, attempting to provide explanations for their actions as a means for establishing a control plane for governing and securing them. Its 100-plus metrics track hallucinations, toxicity, personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, and drift, enforcing policies to protect against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and bias. Enterprises deploy tools like Fiddler to make model drift visible and actionable before it becomes systemic risk . CrowdStrike intends to bundle Fiddler into its flagship platform as Falcon Observe in Q4 FY2027, approximately six months from now, as a means for “proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day,” according to Sentonas’ post announcing the acquisition . CrowdStrike has invested heavily in agentic AI, building an impressive stack of capabilities that extend the Enterprise Graph that made it a dominant player capable of surviving the occasional embarrassing global hiccup . It has even embraced a degree of openness, allowing data ingestion, API connectors, and partnership gateways to enrich the data going into its Falcon AIDR. However, there’s no getting away from Falcon as the single control plane. “CrowdStrike starts with endpoint security and an established enterprise security platform. Other vendors approach the problem through identity, networks, cloud, or security analytics. They all have an incentive to bring customers further into their own platforms,” observes FIOR Group’s Patrick. “The challenge for CrowdStrike, and for every vendor, is that a platform can’t independently verify itself,” he adds. “What’s needed is control that is genuinely independent of any single platform and works across those boundaries.” According to Patrick, a critical feature will be the ability not simply to deploy a security layer but to continuously assess its security and performance. As the traditional detection and remediation stack of cybersecurity is pushed out of shape, the growth in new layers and processes could make this task almost as demanding as the main job of cyber defense that agents were supposed to simplify.

It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given. For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this.

title: Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
raw_text: Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself. The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices. They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities. Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately. The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said. CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said. Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates. Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. “The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson , principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said. Dickson added that security leaders should read the advisory closely, as it calls one flaw “pre-authentication,” then lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.” “Both cannot be true in the usual sense,” he pointed out. Likely access here means being able to reach the admin interface over the network, without a password. “If your admin interface faces the internet, that condition is already met,” Dickson said. The advisory also labels a 9.3 severity rating as “high,” when 9.0 and above is actually “critical” on the standard scale, he pointed out. “These are small things, but labels drive patching queues,” he noted. Also, the advisory does not say whether these flaws are currently being exploited, but it does not say they are not, either. How enterprises should respond “Get the admin interface off the internet,” Dickson emphasized, noting that, as a cybersecurity consultant, he gives that advice at least a handful of times a week. “Management interfaces on edge devices are continually a source of vulnerability .” Once teams limit admin access to a trusted internal network or a dedicated management network, Dickson advised, they should then “verify the patch rather than assume it was properly installed.” From there, he said, analyze for unauthorized visitors by reviewing admin logs, check for unfamiliar accounts, and look for unexpected outbound connections from the device. History matters here, he added. In 2023, after a zero-day on this same email security gateway (ESG), Barracuda told customers with compromised appliances to replace them outright rather than rely on the patch. As he put it: “A patch fixes the lock. It does not tell you who already has a key.” Nelson agreed that enterprises should look closely at who can reach their administrative interfaces. They should, in addition, put access behind additional controls such as a properly configured zero trust access layer. “Exposing those interfaces directly to the internet was always a bad idea,” he said. “As AI makes it easier to find weaknesses and chain attacks together, that exposure becomes increasingly difficult to justify.” AI is also expanding the search for software flaws to include issues such as business logic weaknesses where an application can be made to bypass its intended controls. Authentication and authorization bypasses deserve particular attention in that context, Nelson said. As more vendors use advanced AI to examine their code, CISOs should prepare for more flaw disclosures and potentially shorter windows to respond to them, he noted. “That means identifying exposed appliances, restricting access, and having a response plan ready before the next zero day arrives,” he said. Understanding what each appliance exposes Security appliances are increasingly creating vulnerabilities in corporate networks, which is changing the cybersecurity discussion. Enterprises rely on them to protect the network, yet ultimately they are software systems with vulnerabilities of their own. “They sit exactly where attackers want to be,” Dickson noted. Firewalls, VPNs, and email gateways face the internet by design; that is their job, he said. They see sensitive traffic and hold credentials. Most cannot run the endpoint detection tools that protect laptops and servers, so a compromise can remain undetected for a long time, and every customer runs the same firmware, so one working exploit can scale to thousands of organizations. “The discussion is shifting from which box to buy to what the box itself exposes,” Dickson said. “Every appliance purchase is a decision to trust a vendor’s code at the most exposed point in the network.” It deserves the same scrutiny as any other in an enterprise, he noted. Buyers should ask their vendors four questions, he advised: Is the admin interface exposed to the internet by default; how quickly do patches ship; are they applied automatically; and what logging can users see? “The security appliance does not just protect the perimeter,” Dickson pointed out. “It is the perimeter, and it should be treated as the most attacked system an organization owns, because it is.”
summary: Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself. The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices. They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
raw_text: Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday . “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 , an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.” The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live. Patrick Garrity , the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this. “They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild. “The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks : equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.” Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED. “It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.” Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes. “Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway. Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed. “They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.” Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
raw_text: IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code. Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August . This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities , two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication. Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account. The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale. The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image. “Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.” The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

title: UK organisations warned to brace for AI-powered ransomware attacks
raw_text: AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years. The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses. Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack. AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks. The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks. In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK. “AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts. The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services. Variations on a theme “None of these vectors are radical or new,” said Oliver Spence, CEO of security operations tools vendor CybaVerse. “In fact, they represent the same failures cybercriminals have successfully exploited for decades.” Spence added: “Threat actors rarely depend on the most complex, technical means for launching attacks; more often than not, they search for the most easily exploitable holes in organisations’ systems, like misconfigured VPNs and vulnerabilities in third-party vendor software platforms, and on tried-and-true social engineering techniques.” AI doesn’t represent a sea-change in attackers’ strategies but rather a force multiplier. “Threat actors may be able to leverage AI to launch more sophisticated attacks, but the real danger is in the automated exploitation of existing weaknesses and organisational failures,” Spence concluded. Countermeasures AI offers a means to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but it will only be effective if organisations deal with years of underinvestment and foundational weaknesses before building from a more solid foundation, according to Dr. Horne. The UK government’s Cyber Essentials scheme should become the starting point or baseline for enterprise cyber security, not the end goal, for building improved cyber resilience. Last week the UK government pledged £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, which will be task to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, run by the NCSC.

title: UK government ‘house of cards’ heavily reliant on US AI models
raw_text:
The artificial intelligence (AI) tools used by the UK government rely almost exclusively on models from US tech firms, raising questions over contingency planning.

According to a response to a freedom of information (FOI) request from UK AI firm Aventail, 10 of the 11 AI tools deployed or bought by the Cabinet Office use AI models developed by US tech firms.

title: How to avoid blowing your AI budget
raw_text:
Few CIOs are seeing a return on investment (ROI) from their artificial intelligence (AI) spend. Gartner’s annual worldwide survey found that 58% of CIOs face increased pressure to deliver cost improvements from AI, but at the same time, 51% of them expect AI to increase the total cost of ownership of technology.

According to Gartner analyst Yogesh Bhatt, most enterprises are currently trapped in what he calls a “P&L gap” – P&L meaning profit and loss. In other words, they have no way of accurately measuring the cost of AI against business benefits that directly contribute to an organisation’s profit. 

He said organisations only know how much they have spent on AI when they receive the bill from their AI provider, which can come as “a big shock”.

“What is required,” Bhatt added, “is linking AI FinOps directly to the technical runtime controls. This is an urgent board priority.”

One problem CIOs face is that AI is non-deterministic and cannot be considered, from a software licensing perspective, in the same way as deterministic software like business intelligence (BI) tools, which have very predictable usage patterns.

Listen to the full interview with Yogesh Bhatt in this podcast

“In a more deterministic world, every time you look at a BI dashboard, you’ll get the same responses and insights. But with AI, you are trying to do the reasoning with artificial intelligence and agentic systems, and these are non-deterministic,” said Bhatt.

Since it is non-deterministic, an AI or agentic AI system is not pre-programmed to follow the same set of steps to reach the correct answer. This means AI token consumption – the cost of querying the AI system – can vary. And, as Bhatt warns, cost control gets worse when agentic AI is deployed.

“We overestimate how easily soft productivity gains turn into hard profits, but underestimate how quickly unmonitored agentic workflows burn through the corporate budgets,” he said.

From productivity to value

Choosing which AI tool and large language model (LLM) to adopt is complicated by the fact that enterprise software is littered with AI-enabled products. While some are tightly integrated into enterprise software and aim to tackle specific tasks for users of a particular application, others are positioned for broad adoption.

Mott MacDonald, for instance, has extended a Microsoft pilot to drive AI adoption across the business. It began with a pilot comprising 50 Microsoft Copilot licences, then scaled this to 20,000 people by purchasing a Microsoft 365 E7 subscription for the business nine months ago. To date, Mott MacDonald said 8,000 AI agents have been created.

“We had talked a lot about productivity and doing things faster, especially a year ago,” said Nasrine Tomasi, global head of AI and data at Mott MacDonald. “But we are now going way beyond this, driving up quality and creating value for our clients.”

Mott MacDonald is preparing to use Microsoft Fabric as a central data platform, giving Copilot and its agents better access to the information they need.

The company has built a central AI library, which enables employees looking to develop an agent to discover whether similar agents already exist that can be adapted. Tomasi said Microsoft Agent 365 has been deployed to provide Mott MacDonald with oversight of its growing agent ecosystem. Agent 365 also provides management controls for AI agents to enable what she sees as “enterprise-grade governance”.

Difficult to measure AI productivity gains

“It’s very hard to measure productivity of general roll-out of AI tools,” said Eoin Boylan, head of forward deployed engineering (FDE) at OpenAI. Boylan is part of a 180-person team at OpenAI that works with customers to deliver use cases based on its models. “When we’re working with customers, we’re starting with an outcome, which achieves a transformation that has a measurable business impact,” he said.

Boylan believes that by starting from an outcome, it is easier for organisations to justify AI token costs. “You’re working towards that number, and you’ve agreed on what the return on investment is going to be,” he said. But, in his experience, it is very hard to measure productivity gains when AI tools are rolled out in a more general way across the organisation.

A successful AI deployment also requires an understanding of how work flows through the organisation, the hand-offs to another team, connectivity to different IT systems and where manual data entry is needed. For Boylan, part of the job of an OpenAI FDE is to work alongside the technical team and with business consultants and customers to understand how processes work in the business to enable them to use AI to what he calls “its fullest capabilities”.

The idea that buying an AI tool and deploying it to employees delivers a return on investment is certainly a myth. According to Gartner, IT leaders will need to correlate the costs associated with AI initiatives directly against the company’s P&L accounts, and from a technology perspective, it will be necessary to use fine-grained metrics to monitor the volume of AI tokens being consumed and control excess usage. 

Re-engineering existing workflows will also need to be factored into the ROI, and this may well involve working with external IT and management firms to maximise the chance that the investment in AI pays off in a measurable way, with benefits that directly improve profitability.

title: SailPoint: Anarchy reigns over enterprise agentic AI
raw_text:
Some 89% of enterprises in EMEA have deployed artificial intelligence (AI) agents, but 99% of these lack the identity security tools to govern them, according to research published by identity management supplier SailPoint.

The supplier published the findings from its Horizons of identity security report to coincide with its Navigate conference in London.

The report paints a picture of company networks overrun by anarchistic “machine citizens”, operating outside the rule of law.

Mark McClain, CEO and founder of SailPoint, said in a statement: “Organisations have raced to build highly capable AI agents in production environments to perform complex tasks, creating a classic case of innovation outpacing governance.

“In any society, autonomy without accountability leads to chaos,” he added. “Because agents act independently, access sensitive corporate resources and hold operational privileges, they are active, functioning members of the corporate ecosystem. To transform this digital paradox into secure innovation, the same ‘good citizen’ societal rules that apply to humans must apply to them. Every agent needs a clear owner, full visibility and strict boundaries.”

In an interview with Computer Weekly, he said the explanation for the “big gap” between the deployment of agents and the ability to govern them lies in “the rush to try to gain business advantage from this technology. And now the security industry is trying to catch up, frankly.

“All of this creates a lot of security risk if you don’t understand what you’ve deployed, what kind of access these things have, where they can potentially go,” said McClain. “There’s this term ‘rogue’ out there today. You could argue it’s rogue. You could also argue it was ungoverned, right?

“The [rogue] agents were just trying to accomplish their mission, but because they didn’t have controls and governance around them, they could go do things they really shouldn’t have been allowed to do.”

  • Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Agentic AI governance in the spotlight – during a London event, Microsoft chief Satya Nadella outlined his view of how agentic AI needs to be managed as part of enterprise IT.
  • Agentic AI governance: A Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast – getting tech infrastructure right is just one piece of a complex puzzle that needs to be solved to deploy AI safely in business.

The supplier said what it has identified as a governance gap exists despite regulatory pressures from DORA and the EU AI Act pushing organisations toward greater resilience.

The research also called attention to a “broader lack of readiness. Over half (54%) of all organisations in the EMEA region are still stuck in the earliest, most manual stage of their identity security journey. This leaves them without the centralised controls needed to manage even basic non-human identities, let alone sophisticated AI agents.”

The research was conducted among 340 identity security, IT, cyber security and risk leaders globally, 27% of whom were in the EMEA region.

It found that 22% of enterprises in the region possess mature capabilities for detecting shadow AI, meaning unsanctioned and ungoverned agent deployments. 

It also found that 62% of the worldwide organisations that have invested in securing non-human identities report measurable productivity gains.  

During its Frontier Tour event in London, Microsoft also stressed agent governance. The company’s CEO, Satya Nadella, said he advocated “a set of principles of your trust system.

“I describe them as principles of observability and governance, but you need to identify every agent and you need to be able to log every activity of these agents,” he said.

Nadella said that when an AI agent uses an AI model, it is necessary to log its chain of thought in a human-readable form. This log needs to show that the agent has adhered to the organisation’s governance and compliance rules. And since multiple AI agents may be required to complete a task, each one needs to be uniquely identifiable, he said.

For its part, SailPoint said it has introduced capabilities in its platform “to help move enterprises from chaos to governance, including several classes of agents that organisations can deploy to detect real-time threats and orchestrate other agent classes”.

McClain added: “It is hard to point to any industry that isn’t moving fairly aggressively [with respect to AI and agentic AI]”. In Europe, he said, “there’s a little bit of hesitancy because one of the core value propositions of AI is you can get more efficient and maybe reduce your workforce. In the European continent and in the UK, reducing workforce is a very tricky thing. You’ve got works councils and so on. I don’t think we see that hesitancy in the US.

“My sense is that European companies are trying very much to stay on the front end of technology, just like US companies, just like Asian companies,” said McClain. “So, we’ll see how this adoption works. But there’s not much interest here in cutting the staff through AI. It’s more about productivity gains and doing more.”

title: OECD: AI compute now a strategic asset as UK bets £2bn
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) compute has become a strategic national asset, with venture capital for AI infrastructure more than doubling year-on-year to $123.9bn in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK’s commitment to spend up to £2bn on its Compute Roadmap is one of the leading bets placed by governments around the world.

That’s according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which published its Digital economy and society outlook 2026 today.

In the report, the OECD says AI compute now sits alongside data, algorithms and skills as a determinant of who can build and deploy advanced AI systems. It says venture capital investment in AI firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn in 2024 to $123.9bn in 2025, which is the largest increase since 2012.

The report namechecks the UK Compute Roadmap, launched in 2025 with up to £2bn pledged to “deliver a holistic and user-centred compute ecosystem” and £1bn to expand the AI Research Resource, plus a new national supercomputing service. It also notes the emergence of neocloud providers of infrastructure purpose-built for AI workloads, such as the UK’s Nscale, the US’s CoreWeave and Netherlands-headquartered Nebius.

The OECD is an intergovernmental body whose member governments use it to agree non-binding standards for digital policy. Its reports do not set law, but governments fold their recommendations into regulation – such as the EU AI Act – so the organisation is an early indicator of auditability and data governance requirements that can later become compliance obligations.

The OECD warns in the report that sizeable capital investment in infrastructure, networking and energy access gives traditional hyperscalers a considerable market advantage, which is compounded by developer ecosystems and hardware partnerships that build dependencies. Newer AI-specific providers may expand, it says, but buyers will likely continue to rely on existing hyperscaler capacity – a familiar dynamic for UK organisations balancing cloud lock-in against AI ambition.

The report flags two bottlenecks that may limit compute performance. The first is that accelerator performance has tripled every two years while memory (DRAM) has scaled at just 1.6 times over the same period – a gap it calls “the memory wall”, which can leave processors idle and waiting for data. Moving data between chips forms a second constraint – “the interconnect wall”, which slows distributed training and inference across racks and nodes.

For IT leaders, it says, compute also collides with energy and planning. The OECD notes that hyperscale datacentre buildouts can take up to three years, while securing multi-gigawatt power can take more than four – a mismatch that already shapes grid connection queues and the UK’s push towards 6GW of AI-capable capacity.

“Alongside data, algorithms and skills, AI compute has emerged as a strategic asset with profound implications for innovation and competitiveness,” the report says.

Other government investments in AI include Canada, which committed C$2bn (approx. £1bn) to a Sovereign AI Compute Strategy in 2024; the EU, which will channel €7bn (approx. £5.5bn) through its EuroHPC joint undertaking for 2021-27; and the US, which backs the Stargate datacentre venture.

The OECD report finds that 60% of member countries now assign national digital strategy to a dedicated digital ministry, up from 24% in 2016, and that cyber security has risen to the second-highest policy priority.

The scale of the figures demands caution, the report says. “Figures often reflect announcements and commitments rather than implementation,” it says, with delivery dependent on supply chain resilience, energy and water availability, and shifting national priorities.

On that reading, the investment surge can be viewed as a statement of intent rather than evidence of built capacity. Turning the UK’s £2bn into operational infrastructure will depend on grid and planning constraints that decide whether promised datacentres arrive on time.
