title: Capita last UK firm among government strategic tech suppliers
raw_text:
Capita is now the only UK-headquartered company among the 12 tech firms on the UK government’s strategic suppliers list. The other 11 technology suppliers on the list – Accenture, Atos, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Capgemini, CGI, DXC Technology, Fujitsu, IBM, Microsoft, Oracle and Sopra Steria – are headquartered outside the UK.

The finding comes from Tussell’s ninth UK strategic suppliers report, which found public sector spending with the group reached £5.48bn in the 2025/26 financial year.

Those suppliers are among the UK government’s 36 strategic suppliers, which are split across technology (12), engineering and construction (7), outsourcing and facilities management (5), aerospace and defence (5), consulting (4) and telecoms (3). Capita’s position as the last UK tech supplier follows the removal of three firms from the list in 2026 – two of them UK-headquartered, including the IT reseller Computacenter.

Capgemini is the largest tech supplier by FY25/26 spend, with £940m, ahead of IBM on £653m and Capita on £639m. Sopra Steria (£571m), Atos (£551m) and Accenture (£442m) follow, with Fujitsu (£388m), CGI (£374m), Oracle (£355m) and AWS (£350m) close behind. Microsoft (£124m) and DXC Technology (£92m) complete the dozen – a spread from £940m to £92m.

The figures cover direct spend only. Sales through resellers and channel partners are excluded, so Microsoft, Oracle and AWS – which sell heavily through the channel – are under-represented, and their true public sector footprint is larger than this ranking shows.

Who are the UK’s strategic suppliers?

Strategic suppliers are private companies the Cabinet Office judges so critical to public services that it coordinates their relationship with government centrally. Each has had a Crown Representative since 2011, and since 2019, suppliers have had to sign a memorandum of understanding that puts the onus on them to report risk. Designation is not a spend ranking, though these firms typically take more than £100m a year from government.

The 36 suppliers, as of 1 July 2026, span six sectors:

  • Technology (12)
  • Engineering and construction (7)
  • Outsourcing & facilities management (5)
  • Aerospace and defence (5)
  • Consulting (4)
  • Telecoms (3)

The list reflects direct, centrally managed relationships, and excludes reseller and channel sales: Google Cloud does not appear at all, while AWS, Microsoft and Oracle are judged on direct spend rather than their full public sector footprint.

Central government accounts for the bulk of the tech spend, at £3.84bn. The NHS spends £600m with the 12, local government £286m, transport £264m, defence £250m and blue-light services £214m.

The £5.48bn is a floor. Several large buyers – including the Ministry of Justice, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and NHS England – had not published full FY25/26 invoice data when Tussell extracted the figures in August 2026, and part of Ministry of Defence spending is exempt from publication for national security reasons.

According to Tussell, British firms’ share of overall strategic supplier spend fell from 65% to 61% since FY20/21. Spending with the big four consultancies – Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC – dropped by 15% in real terms in the same period. Kier and Balfour Beatty now take 59% of construction spending with the sector’s strategic suppliers, up from 33%.

Technology is the only strategic supplier sector that’s growing.

The tech list matters because these are contracts that carry the government’s most critical digital programmes. Eleven foreign-headquartered firms and one British firm concentrate delivery in a small group of suppliers, raise exit costs on long-running contracts, and leave little room for UK suppliers to break into the top tier. That matters most where a system runs for a decade or more, since switching suppliers on a live tax, benefits or health platform is slow, costly and politically fraught.

Individual buying patterns show how narrow that base can be. Fujitsu’s £388m comes mostly from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC), with £267m, and the Home Office, with £58m. AWS, on £350m, draws £124m from HMRC and £86m from the Home Office. Capita’s £639m spreads across the Department for Work and Pensions (£148m), Transport for London (£147m) and the Department for Education (£65m), with a long tail of councils and departments behind them.

On the list, Fujitsu remains under scrutiny for its part in the Post Office Horizon scandal. The government’s dependence on a fixed set of large suppliers is visible elsewhere too, from police forces’ reliance on hyperscale cloud to the rush of artificial intelligence (AI) procurement that has handed Palantir £553m.

For UK tech firms, losing ground among the government’s most important suppliers narrows the domestic base that British suppliers can sell into, at a time when ministers want more home-grown capability in cloud and AI.

The tension is that public sector tech spending is rising in value as the supplier base thins in national headquarters, at a time when the government is talking up sovereign capability and support for UK suppliers.

title: Mastercard meets ‘responsibility’ through SME cyber security training
raw_text:
Mastercard has launched free cyber security training to UK small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as the firm’s own research reveals over three million of them don’t use cyber security.

With SMEs being targeted by cyber criminals and many going out of business as a result, the card giant’s UK boss says financial services firms have a responsibility to pass knowledge to SMEs.

Over five million UK SMEs will have access to the resources through SME Academy: Cybersecurity, which Mastercard’s UK division president, Simon Forbes, said offers “short, practical, free modules on the threats owners face most, so they can protect their business and keep growing”.

The plan is to expand the programme to more than 10 million SMEs across Europe by 2030.

Quoting government figures, Forbes said cyber crime costs UK business more than £14bn a year, adding that small businesses often have the least protection.

“The payments and technology sector has spent decades learning how criminals operate, and with attacks in the UK more than doubling in a year, we have a responsibility to put that knowledge to work,” he told Computer Weekly.

In a recent SME report, Mastercard found that fewer than 39% of UK small businesses use basic cyber security tools such as antivirus software and firewalls. 

Furthermore, according to data from the government’s Cyber security breaches survey 2025/26, 46% of SMEs were targeted by cyber criminals in a 12-month period, with nearly 18% going bankrupt following a cyber attack.

Mastercard’s SME Academy: Cybersecurity features modules on how to recognise increasingly sophisticated phishing attempts and how data breaches happen. It also provides learning on strengthening passwords and using multi-factor authentication, as well as managing employee and third-party access among other training.

Sonny Leong, minister for small business and enterprise, said: “We have so many innovative small businesses in this country, yet cyber crime remains one of the biggest threats to their success.

“Mastercard’s SME Academy is a very welcome initiative that will help businesses stay well ahead of criminals, working with industry leaders to help equip them with the tools and support they need to thrive and grow our economy.”

Forbes at Mastercard added: “Every small business starts with a dream, but cyber security risks can quickly turn it into a nightmare. Nearly 20% of small businesses don’t survive a cyber attack. Keeping pace with constantly evolving technology and threats is difficult, particularly when time and resources are stretched. Our SME Academy offers clear, practical advice to help business owners take steps today to protect the dream they’ve worked so hard to build.”

In a sign of increasing threats, earlier this week, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of GCHQ, warned the UK will face AI-powered attacks from nation-states and criminal groups targeting critical national infrastructure in the next two years.

The use of AI by hostile states and crime groups is expected to increase the scale and speed of ransomware attacks, social engineering and the exploitation of vulnerabilities.

The NCSC said Russia and China will routinely use AI-powered cyber tools to achieve their geopolitical goals.

title: The invisible maths behind cloud carbon accounting
raw_text:
Enterprise carbon dashboards offer a soothing narrative. Every month, CIOs receive automated reports that show declining Scope 2 emissions, falling carbon intensity per virtual core, and steady progress towards net-zero targets. 

For any platform engineer tasked with auditing actual operational efficiency, however, these numbers resemble financial engineering rather than physical measurement. Measuring and offsetting carbon reduction in the public cloud remains an elusive goal because the underlying architecture is deliberately built to conceal physical reality from the tenant.

Multi-tenancy defines cloud economics. Hypervisors abstract physical hardware so virtual machines and container runtimes share silicon cores, L3 caches, memory controllers, and network fabric. Cloud carbon calculators estimate emissions by multiplying virtual CPU hours or storage gigabytes against static regional emission factors. 

That top-down estimation collapses under technical scrutiny. A containerised microservice can spike CPU utilisation on a shared physical socket while sitting adjacent to a high-draw workload. 

Because the hypervisor pools resource allocation dynamically, customers lack access to core-level power telemetry. An organisation cannot accurately reduce or offset a carbon metric its infrastructure provider refuses to expose.

The grid reality and market-based illusions

The measurement gap widens when examining how hyperscalers account for electrical energy. 

Under corporate greenhouse gas protocols, organisations report Scope 2 emissions using two distinct methodologies. Market-based accounting permits cloud providers to claim zero-carbon operations by purchasing annual power purchase agreements or unbundled energy attribute certificates. Meanwhile, location-based accounting reflects the actual fossil fuels burning in the local grid at the exact second a workload executes.

If a firm in London runs a heavy data processing pipeline at midnight in a region powered primarily by gas generation, the physical servers draw high-carbon electricity straight from the wall. 

But market-based accounting wipes those emissions away on the monthly invoice. This annual matching model creates a dangerous illusion of progress. An organisation can satisfy corporate sustainability audits while burning fossil fuels at the physical substation. Without hourly, location-based carbon data tied directly to workload execution, calculating genuine operational reduction is mathematically impossible.

The hidden impact of embodied carbon and hardware lifecycles

Operational electricity tells only half the story. The environmental footprint most glaringly omitted from enterprise cloud accounting is embodied carbon, which represents the massive energy debt incurred long before a server ever boots up. Fabricating silicon wafers, etching microarchitecture, manufacturing high-bandwidth memory, and assembling server chassis require extreme temperatures and rare earth extraction, which commit a heavy carbon toll before hardware enters a datacentre.

Cloud providers traditionally amortise this manufacturing footprint over a standardised depreciation schedule of four to six years, but the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators has shattered that model. 

Hyperscalers are refreshing GPU fleets every two to three years to keep pace with machine learning demands, and massively accelerating embodied carbon debt per rack. Standard cloud carbon reporting tools rarely adjust downstream Scope 3 metrics in real time based on this accelerated hardware churn. Enterprises inherit the emissions of rapidly discarded infrastructure without seeing the true lifecycle cost reflected in their monthly bills.

Ephemeral workload migration and unstable baselines

Establishing a stable baseline for reduction is equally difficult in environments defined by constant motion. Modern cloud architectures feature Kubernetes clusters that auto-scale across nodes, serverless functions that spin up for milliseconds, and cloud control planes that routinely live-migrate virtual machines across physical racks to balance loads or execute maintenance.

When workloads shift across availability zones or distant geographical regions based on spot-market pricing, grid carbon intensity fluctuates instantly. A workload executed on a hydro-powered grid in Scotland yesterday might run on a gas-heavy grid in the Midlands today. 

Without immutable workload placement and fixed regional baselines, to prove that a software optimisation actually reduced carbon, rather than merely riding a shift in dynamic cloud routing, remains speculative. Developers have zero direct control over where their compute lands unless they enforce rigid and expensive node affinity rules.

Solving cloud sustainability requires moving past high-level billing approximations. Until cloud providers expose raw, core-level power telemetry, align carbon reporting with real-time hourly grid matching, and transparently account for accelerated hardware lifecycle churn, cloud carbon accounting will remain an administrative fiction. Enterprises cannot manage what their infrastructure providers hide behind layers of abstraction.

title: UK government responds to facial recognition consultation
raw_text:
The UK government has reiterated its intention to bring forward a new legislative framework for police use of biometrics, but has so far refrained from committing to specific safeguards.

In December 2025, the Home Office launched a 10-week consultation on police use of biometrics, including live facial recognition (LFR), allowing interested parties and members of the public to share their views on how the controversial technology should be regulated.

This followed on from then-home secretary Yvette Cooper telling a Lords committee in July 2025 that the government intended to create “a proper, clear governance framework” to regulate the use of facial recognition technology by police.

When launching the consultation, the Home Office said that although a “patchwork” legal framework for police use of facial recognition technology exists – including for increasing use of retrospective and “operator-initiated” versions – it does not give police forces the confidence to “use it at significantly greater scale … nor does it consistently give the public the confidence that it will be used responsibly”.

It added that the current rules governing police LFR use are “complicated and difficult to understand”, and that an ordinary member of the public would be required to read four pieces of legislation, police national guidance documents and a range of detailed legal or data protection documents from individual forces to fully understand the basis for LFR use on their high streets.

Now, responding to the consultation – which closed nine months ago, in February 2026 – the government has summarised the views received and set out high-level proposals for a new legal framework.

The government said the framework “will ensure policing can innovate in a repeatable and consistent manner, supporting adoption of emerging biometric and overt surveillance technologies that improve policing effectiveness and public protection, while maintaining appropriate safeguards and oversight”.

It will also establish a new independent oversight body, which will consolidate and expand the functions of existing oversight roles, as well as be empowered to monitor compliance and enforce standards.

Promise of stronger safeguards around biometrics falls short

However, the consultation response lacks detail on what specific safeguards the government is considering, and how it will address wider concerns around bias and discrimination, proportionality and necessity (a key legal test for UK police), the protection of freedom of expression, and scope creep (where use of the tech goes beyond its original purpose).

“The Home Office’s facial recognition consultation raised important questions about how police protect the privacy of people, of innocent bystanders, and the government is right to bring a wider range of visual AI technologies under statutory oversight,” said Simon Randall, CEO of visual data privacy company Pimloc.

“But promising safeguards isn’t the same as spelling them out. The government has yet to explain who can access the data, how it can be shared or reused, and how long it can be kept. Until those limits are clear, it’s difficult to see how the promised safeguards will work in practice.”

Tony Kounnis, CEO of Face Int UK, added that although the government’s promise to introduce stronger safeguards is a step in the right direction, it “falls short” of where policy needs to go.

“We need more robust rules in place to ensure companies developing and deploying facial recognition technology are doing enough to protect data,” he said. “Privacy by design must be the mantra, and the government cannot dawdle in tackling this issue.”

Akiko Hart, director of human rights group Liberty, said legal safeguards are long overdue, and called on the government to stop expanding police use of biometrics until these are in place.

“Millions of people have had their faces scanned without their consent. We’ve seen people hauled out of their homes after being misidentified by racially biased algorithms, and facial recognition deployments are fast becoming a fixture on our high streets, at football matches and music events,” she said.

“While the announcement that new safeguards will be introduced is a step in the right direction, now that the government has recognised stronger legislation is needed, it must finally hit pause on the rapid roll-out of facial recognition technology until this is in place with the robust transparency, oversight and safeguards needed to protect us all.”

Vague responses to concerns shared

Within the 1,826 unique responses to the government consultation, prevalent concerns revolved around data handling and retention, protecting civil liberties and public participation, trust in police and the state, and the potential for mass surveillance.

According to the government summary of the responses received, civil liberties concerns largely revolved around the potentially chilling effect of biometric surveillance, which could deter people’s lawful and free use of public space due to a “discomfort with constant observation” and prevent them from “participation in civic life” due to the psychological impacts such an atmosphere would create.

“Those respondents raising civil liberties issues often said facial recognition should be prohibited at protests and demonstrations, fearing it could be used to target or discourage participants,” it said. “Advocacy groups warned this could disproportionately affect marginalised communities and further damage trust in law enforcement.”

It further highlighted how respondents were concerned that biometric surveillance could undermine the presumption of innocence and lead the state to treat the general population as potential suspects.

“Others argued that innocent individuals should not be routinely included in watchlists, and that expanding biometric databases, such as through passport images, posed serious democratic risks by normalising monitoring, shifting power towards the state and weakening public trust,” it noted.

“Respondents [also] raised concerns that facial recognition could be used beyond its original purpose and evolve into routine mass surveillance without binding limits. Some feared misuse by future governments, including for monitoring dissent, political opposition, or excluding individuals from public spaces.”

Responding to these concerns, the government said it agrees that “technologies like facial recognition have the potential to interfere with rights, such as the right to privacy, freedom of expression and the right to peaceful assembly”, which is why it intends to “introduce new, specific laws governing their use”.

However, it did not provide any detail on how the specific concerns raised could be addressed, simply noting that the framework will include “detailed operational requirements and safeguards in a statutory Code of Practice” and “balance the need to respect and preserve individual human rights with the rights of the public to be safe on the streets and in their communities”.

Necessary and proportionate?

Other areas of concern revolved around whether deployments of biometric technologies would be both necessary and proportionate, with “many respondents” arguing that biometric technologies should only be used by police “where there is a demonstrable operational need and where less intrusive methods would be ineffective”.

It further noted that some believe the technologies should not be used under any circumstances because of their “concerns about accuracy, bias and broader societal impacts”, while others “accepted limited use, particularly in serious or time-critical situations” provided strong safeguards were in place.

Critics have previously highlighted the “catch net” nature of LFR surveillance, the inclusion of people in watchlists for minor offences like shoplifting that do not meet the legal threshold of serious criminality, and the selection of watchlist images based on crime categories attached to custody photos rather than a context-specific assessment of the threat presented by a given individual.

Successive biometrics commissioners have also highlighted the Home Office’s ongoing unlawful retention of millions of custody images in the Police National Database (PND), which serves as the main source of facial images for police watchlists.

The government said in its consultation response that while it “believes that biometric, facial recognition and similar technologies are valuable tools in tackling serious crime and enhancing public safety”, it also recognises “they should only be used when necessary, proportionate and justified”.

It added: “We believe that the seriousness of the crime should not be the sole criterion for assessing whether the deployment of the technologies is necessary and proportionate but instead that it must be considered alongside other factors including the scale and nature of the deployment and the impact on individual rights. The law will require justification according to specific criteria and consideration of detailed guidance.”

On whether the framework should also apply to the private sector, the government said it acknowledged the appetite for greater consistency between law enforcement and private sector use of biometrics, and committed to bringing forward a code of practice for private sector use that would complement the law enforcement-specific framework.

Pressing ahead without a framework

While the use of LFR by police – beginning with the Met’s deployment at Notting Hill Carnival in August 2016 – has ramped up substantially in recent years, there has so far been minimal public debate or consultation, with the Home Office claiming for years that there is already a “comprehensive” legal framework in place.

In that time, there have been repeated calls from Parliament and civil society for the use of facial recognition by police to be regulated.

This includes three separate inquiries by the Justice and Home Affairs Committee into shoplifting, police algorithms and police facial recognition; two of the UK’s former biometrics commissioners, Paul Wiles and Fraser Sampson; an independent legal review by Matthew Ryder QC; the UK’s Equalities and Human Rights Commission; and the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, which called for a moratorium on live facial recognition as far back as July 2019.

However, despite coming to recognise the need for a new legal framework and launching a consultation on the matter in December 2025, the government has pressed ahead with expanding use of biometric technologies.

Before the consultation had even closed, for example, the Home Office announced sweeping reform to UK policing in January 2026, which included significant investment in the LFR capabilities of police in England and Wales.

Since then, the Met Police has pushed ahead with a major expansion of facial recognition technology, committing in June 2026 to the deployment of static LFR cameras fixed to street furniture in the West End and Soho by the end of the year, which followed a pilot of this approach in Croydon.

In March 2026, the force also started to trial handheld facial recognition technology that will allow officers to conduct biometric checks on the spot.

Computer Weekly also reported on 30 October 2026 that UK Immigration Enforcement is also set to start deploying LFR technology outside of border zones to look for people who have never committed a criminal offence.

title: Saudi Arabia’s digital sports expansion creates new cyber security challenges
raw_text:
Saudi Arabia’s accelerating investment in sport is creating a cyber security challenge as clubs and sporting organisations adopt connected technologies, digital fan engagement platforms and services powered by artificial intelligence (AI).

Under the Kingdom’s Vision 2030 programme, sport has become an increasingly important part of its economic diversification and digital transformation ambitions. However, the expansion of digital services is also exposing organisations to a broader range of cyber threats, including compromised accounts, data exposure and attacks targeting connected venue infrastructure.

According to Sultan Alanazi, country regional director for Saudi Arabia at LogRhythm | Exabeam, the growing complexity of sports organisations’ technology environments is making it harder for security teams to distinguish legitimate activity from potentially malicious behaviour.

“Areas including ticketing, fan services and venue systems are now more connected, increasing the risk of personal data exposure, cyber attacks targeting supporters, and disruption to the services clubs use to serve them,” he said.

One emerging challenge is the potential misuse of legitimate access credentials. A compromised account may already have authorised access to ticketing platforms, customer databases or other operational systems, making suspicious activity more difficult to identify through conventional security monitoring.

Introducing AI agents into business operations adds another dimension to this risk. As sports organisations experiment with autonomous systems to support performance analysis and administrative processes, agents may be granted access to sensitive information and enterprise tools.

“Areas including ticketing, fan services and venue systems are now more connected, increasing the risk of personal data exposure, cyber attacks targeting supporters, and disruption to the services clubs use to serve them”

Sultan Alanazi, LogRhythm | Exabeam

However, Alanazi warned that authorised access does not necessarily mean an agent will always behave as intended. 

An AI agent could exceed its assigned remit, retrieve information beyond its intended purpose or be manipulated by an attacker. This creates a new category of insider risk, in which potentially harmful activity originates from an authorised digital entity rather than an external threat actor.

“AI agents add to the region’s risk environment as clubs explore their uses within the sports sector without proper governance and threat detection,” he said. “These agents introduce another form of insider risk.”

Connected stadiums expand the attack surface

The risks extend beyond the digital platforms used to engage supporters. Sports organisations are increasingly dependent on interconnected environments spanning ticketing, payments, player performance systems, cloud applications and physical venue infrastructure.

Internet of things (IoT) devices, including turnstiles, surveillance cameras and building management systems, can introduce additional entry points into corporate networks, particularly when different teams or external providers are responsible for managing them.

Alanazi said the growing number of connections between sensitive data, users, applications and third-party providers makes it increasingly difficult for security teams to establish whether access is appropriate.

Player health and performance records, for example, may be shared across multiple departments and applications. As the number of access points increases, organisations need greater visibility into who is accessing information, why it is being accessed and whether that activity falls within expected parameters.

Similarly, a compromised account used to manage connected venue technology could potentially provide an attacker with a route into other connected systems.

Regional geopolitical tensions add further pressure to an environment in which sporting organisations need to maintain operational continuity and protect sensitive information.

Strengthening threat monitoring, detection and response

These challenges are informing a memorandum of understanding between LogRhythm | Exabeam and Saudi football club Al Qadsiah, which aims to explore opportunities to strengthen the club’s threat monitoring, detection and incident response capabilities.

The collaboration will examine three areas that Alanazi identifies as common weaknesses in organisations beginning to develop their cyber security operations: fragmented visibility, limited contextual information and unclear responsibilities.

Fragmented visibility occurs when activity across business networks, cloud environments and venue technology is monitored through separate systems. Without the ability to correlate events across these environments, security analysts may struggle to establish the full scope of an incident.

Limited context presents another problem. An alert may indicate that an account has accessed a particular system, but provide little information about who or what initiated the activity, whether it was expected or what happened afterwards.

This becomes particularly significant as organisations introduce AI agents that can carry out tasks alongside human employees.

The third challenge is governance. Organisations need clearly defined responsibilities for investigating alerts, involving external service providers and authorising action when a digital service is at risk. For Alanazi, the ability to establish these responsibilities is essential to moving beyond threat detection towards a coordinated security response.

Insider threats and AI governance move up the agenda

The growing cyber security requirements of the sports sector come as Saudi organisations increasingly adopt AI across their operations.

Research from LogRhythm | Exabeam, titled From adoption to accountability, found that 75% of Saudi respondents claimed AI was already improving the speed and accuracy of their security operations. However, another report from the company, From human to hybrid: How AI and the analytics gap are fueling insider risk, found that 70% of cyber security professionals in the Middle East viewed malicious or compromised insiders as a greater threat than external attackers.

Alanazi said these findings highlight the need for organisations to develop stronger behavioural monitoring capabilities as their technology environments become more complex.

While cyber security investment in Saudi Arabia has traditionally concentrated on critical infrastructure sectors such as banking, energy and government, he argued that sporting organisations should not be overlooked.

A cyber incident involving a high-profile club could expose supporters’ personal information, disrupt commercial operations and undermine public trust. As clubs introduce more digital services and connect additional users and systems, their exposure to insider threats also increases.

AI-powered security operations need human oversight

AI is also becoming an increasingly prominent component of the security technologies being deployed to address these challenges. However, Alanazi said its value should be measured by its ability to improve investigation and response processes rather than by the technology itself.

AI can help security analysts prioritise alerts, collect relevant evidence and summarise investigations, allowing teams to concentrate on incidents that pose the greatest risk.

The company’s Nova AI capabilities are intended to support analysts in investigating incidents and determining which activity requires attention. Its partnership with Google Cloud also provides organisations with a way to apply behavioural analytics to data held within Google Security Operations.

However, Alanazi cautioned against treating AI deployment as an end in itself: “Clubs should assess the value of AI based on outcomes that include faster investigations and more consistent responses,” he said.

He added that reliable data, clear governance and human oversight remain essential, with analysts ultimately responsible for assessing findings and making decisions.

The company is also planning a customer innovation centre in Riyadh, as part of an expanded regional headquarters expected to open in the fourth quarter of 2026. The facility is intended to help organisations explore how AI technologies can be deployed securely in operational environments.

Security by design for Saudi sport

As Saudi Arabia continues to invest in sporting infrastructure and digital services under Vision 2030, Alanazi said cyber security needs to be incorporated into technology projects from the outset rather than treated as an additional requirement after deployment.

This includes involving security teams in business decisions, assessing the security implications of new services and establishing clear ownership before systems go live.

AI agents require particular attention, with organisations needing to define the tasks they can perform, the information and tools they can access, and which actions require human approval.

Also, as connected venues, digital fan platforms and AI-driven services become more central to the Kingdom’s sporting ambitions, the ability to monitor activity across these environments will be an increasingly important part of operational resilience.

“Ensuring security decisions are a fundamental part of each project’s design, approval and review process gives clubs a responsible way to grow their AI capabilities under Saudi Vision 2030,” said Alanazi.

title: Data dive: Datacentre electricity – how much, where, why regions matter
raw_text:
The UK’s datacentres used 1.8% of all Great Britain’s grid electricity in 2024. That proportion had increased from 1.2% in 2020. That electricity draw was heavily concentrated, with Slough and Hillingdon together drawing nearly three times that of the North, Midlands, Scotland, the South West and Wales combined.

Meanwhile, as computing got more intensive alongside the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), datacentre electricity consumption increased by 41% while the datacentre count rose by only 8%. That means each datacentre counted became 31% hungrier.

That’s all according to data published by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) and analysed here by Computer Weekly. Datacentres are one of the few sectors that still add demand to the grid. Total electricity demand in Great Britain is essentially flat. DESNZ’s Digest of UK energy statistics records 2025 demand of 323TWh (terawatt-hours), which was below pre-pandemic 2019 levels.

Renewables generated a record 153TWh in 2025, a 52.1% share of all generation. Fossil fuels, meanwhile, generated 94.9TWh in the first full year without coal. A datacentre estate that draws 4.46TWh consumes about a fifth of everything Britain’s solar panels produced in 2025. Meanwhile, industrial consumption fell for a fourth consecutive year to 76.7TWh, its lowest since 1983. Domestic consumption sat at 96.2TWh and commercial consumption at 67.9TWh.

In this article, we look at datacentre electricity demand, how it is growing, where it has grown and how its growth has become more concentrated in particular regions. We also look at how AI compute has seen the power draw per site become denser.

TL;DR – UK datacentre electricity in five numbers

  • Datacentres drew 4.46TWh from the grid in 2024 – 1.8% of all gigabyte electricity, up 41% since 2020.
  • Slough’s datacentres use 65.2% of the borough’s electricity; Hillingdon’s datacentre load grew 407% in four years.
  • Slough and Hillingdon together draw nearly three times that of the North, Midlands, Scotland, South West and Wales combined.
  • Consumption rose 41% while the datacentre count rose only 8% – each unit is 31% hungrier.
  • The North (-20%), Midlands (-24%) and Scotland (-11%) all shrank in terms of electricity draw.

Where the power goes

DESNZ splits its estimates by area, and that distribution is a big part of the story. Nearly all recent growth concentrates in west London and the M4 corridor, while most of the country is going in the other direction.

Slough’s datacentres consumed 1.29TWh in 2024 – 65.2% of the borough’s grid electricity, up from 44.4% in 2020. Hillingdon’s datacentre share of the borough’s grid electricity climbed from 7.4% to 28.1% over the same period, with Tower Hamlets, home to the Docklands colocation hub, drawing 18.2% of the borough’s grid electricity. Between them, datacentres in Slough and Hillingdon drew 1.83TWh – nearly three times as much as those in the North, Midlands, Scotland, South West and Wales combined, at 0.68TWh.

The growth is just as lopsided. Hillingdon’s datacentre consumption rose by 407% between 2020 and 2024, Outer London by 85% and the South East by 57%, while the South West and Wales rose by 107% from a small base. The direction reverses elsewhere. The North fell by 20%, the Midlands 24%, Scotland 11%, and the rest of the South East – the commuter belt beyond the M4’s core – by 22%, while Hampshire rose by 23% and Greater Manchester was broadly flat. The much-discussed regional build-out is not visible in the electricity data.

The geography results from where fibre is most dense and interconnection points sit, which is why the Slough-Hillingdon axis and London’s Docklands have anchored the UK’s colocation industry for two decades.

The much-discussed regional build-out is not visible in this electricity data, but it dates from 2020-2024, so perhaps redressing that imbalance explains more recent initiatives such as AI growth zones.

The divergence between sites and power reveals the roll-out of newer, denser and more power-hungry AI compute. DESNZ counted 239 operational datacentres in 2024, up from 221 in 2020. That was a rise of only 8%, but it is set against a 41% rise in electricity consumption.

The average metered site drew about 14.3GWh in 2020 and 18.7GWh in 2024, a 31% increase. New datacentres are more numerous but lots hungrier on a per-site basis. That’s the signature of hyperscale and AI-era builds that pack more compute and more cooling into each data hall. A single modern AI aisle can draw more power than an entire older colocation facility, which is why count and consumption diverge, and a nearly flat site count can hide a steep rise in consumption.

DESNZ’s count of 239 deserves scrutiny. It built its dataset by matching electricity meters to a compiled register of datacentres, and counted each campus building separately. Computer Weekly’s analysis of the government’s Energy Performance Certificate registers found roughly 90 to 110 datacentre sites across England, Wales and Scotland after manual verification. That is less than half the DESNZ figure, but likely maps to the fact that many datacentres counted by Computer Weekly comprise multiple metered buildings.

The methodology behind the data

The DESNZ estimate matches meter-level electricity consumption – the same data used for its subnational electricity statistics – to a list of datacentres, and counts a facility as operational only if at least one meter matched. It covers colocation, managed hosting and hyperscale datacentres, and explicitly excludes enterprise facilities owned and run for an organisation’s own IT. That means the 4.46TWh and 1.8% figures are a floor that leaves out private enterprise datacentres.

DESNZ notes that the estimates carry uncertainty. Some regions are combined, and a facility only counts as operational if a meter can be matched to it. The percentage-of-grid figures are measured against each area’s own electricity consumption, which is why they spike where the local denominator is small – Slough’s datacentres draw nearly two-thirds of a borough that has relatively little else that draws power.

Britain’s electricity use curve is flat to falling. Demand is below 2019 levels, and industrial consumption is at its lowest since 1983. Meanwhile, renewables push to a record share of generation. DESNZ’s 4.46TWh equates to about 4.6% of domestic electricity use (96.2TWh in 2025). So, a sector that adds 41% in four years – and concentrates it in a single corridor – is the exception to an overall decline.

That concentration of demand evident in the DESNZ data runs against the geography of the current build-out. Computer Weekly’s tracking of committed pipeline counts more than 14GW of planned capacity, with the largest schemes heading for the North East and Scotland. That’s probably a good thing because the grid access that London and the M4 corridor lack is exactly what the regions can offer.

The UK’s datacentres used 1.8% of all Great Britain’s grid electricity in 2024. That proportion had increased from 1.2% in 2020. That electricity draw was heavily concentrated, with Slough and Hillingdon together drawing nearly three times that of the North, Midlands, Scotland, the South West and Wales combined.

title: MPs launch civil service pension investigation but won’t rely on Capita data and promises
raw_text:
MPs on the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) have launched an inquiry into the botched civil service pension scheme (CSPS) administration, but will use factual data from the spending watchdog and not rely on Capita. 

This comes almost exactly a year after the PAC’s findings that there was a “real risk” Capita would not be ready to take over the administration of the CSPS in December 2025 as planned.

At the time, the outsourcer hit back, claiming the PAC’s statement was “not reflective of the current state of the transition”, and inaccurate. But despite having years to prepare for the pension scheme, just a month after Capita took over in December 2025, an HMRC troubleshooter was brought in to lead an “urgent recovery plan” as the scheme experienced difficulties. There are retired civil servants still waiting for their pensions a year on, and many are suffering severe financial hardship.

The PAC’s latest inquiry follows three separate evidence sessions where Capita has made promises to MPs that they have gone on to break, according to the committee chair.

PAC chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown MP said: “Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong.”

The subsequent loss of trust has engendered a move away from relying on Capita figures, with MPs to use data from the National Audit Office (NAO), which announced its own investigation into the CSPS failings last month. “… we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this committee,” said Clifton-Brown.

The move to use NAO figures rather than rely on Capita’s has been welcomed by CSPS members, who have waited many months for their pensions and suffered financial hardship as a result of Capita’s failings.

Welcomed independence

The Civil Service Pensions Campaign group, set up in the wake of the disaster to support scheme members, said: “We welcome the PAC’s decision to launch a further inquiry, particularly its commitment to base its scrutiny on independent findings from the NAO, rather than relying on Capita’s own performance figures and assurances.

“It has been clear since December 2025 that the experiences of our members bear little resemblance to the picture repeatedly presented by Capita and the Cabinet Office. We have been raising these concerns for the past seven months, yet members continue to face unacceptable delays, financial hardship and considerable distress.”

Steve Tessier, a retired civil servant who spent most of his career at the Ministry of Defence, as well as a spell on secondment at Nato, has waited a year for his pension. He said the PACs decision to avoid Capita data “is a massive vote of no confidence in Capita. And if we can’t trust Capita’s management info, what else should we discount, and by how much?

“The PAC has recognised what scheme members have been saying for months: Capita’s figures bear no relation to reality,” he added. “If only those in authority – especially the Cabinet Office – had paid closer attention sooner, we might be further down the road to recovery.”

Capita ‘delusional’

A Public and Commercial Services Union rep working on the contract said: “The progress Capita keep advertising seems to be delusional.”

The union said one major issue was the switch from the MyCSP IT system to Capita’s. It said members report it being “slow, unstable and not intuitive”.

It reported a member as stating: “I feel like we have gone back in time. The system is dated and crashes a lot.”

Staff are having to work manually from spreadsheets, according to the union.

For its inquiry, The PAC will be taking its own written and oral evidence.

The Civil Service Pensions Campaign group said the government also has questions to answer. “The question must be asked: why has the Cabinet Office been so willing to accept Capita’s assurances at face value when the evidence from those directly affected has consistently told a very different story?”

In September, the Cabinet Office announced it was setting up a function to check the CSPS data provided by Capita, to reduce its reliance on the outsourcing provider’s data.

The campaign group added that while it welcomes inquiries and investigations to get to the truth, the priority should be getting former civil servants the pensions they are owed. “Independent scrutiny is long overdue, but it must lead to accountability and meaningful action,” it said. “Members cannot afford to wait for another report while their pensions remain unpaid.”

title: TSB releases shocking fraud data to urge caution as Black Friday and Christmas near
raw_text:
TSB customer data has revealed that 45% of money lost through bank transfer fraud was the result of purchase scams.

The bank has released data from between the beginning of this year and the end of September, which showed customers lost £2.6m to online purchase fraud during the period. It also found that two-thirds of the scams came via Facebook.

Purchase fraud, which sees fake or non-existent goods advertised on online platforms, accounts for nearly half of the losses to transfer fraud suffered by TSB customers. The bank’s data found that Facebook accounted for 65% of scams, followed by TikTok (14%) and Snapchat (7%). 

Because the payments are authorised by the customers, the banks cannot use security systems to block them, but can advise them. TSB is releasing the headline figures to warn customers and urge them to be “vigilant” as the festive season approaches.

“Alarmingly, purchase fraud is a growing problem – so we’re urging consumers to be especially careful where and who they shop with as we enter the busy sales, and Christmas shopping period,” said Richard Daniels, director of fraud prevention at TSB.

“The sheer scale of shopping scams shows that you just can’t fully trust a seller online – so be cautious and consider sticking to official sites, or marketplaces that offer a payment platform,” he added. 

TSB revealed that vehicle and holiday/flights were the most scammed purchases, accounting for average losses of about £1,500 and £1,200, respectively.

Car parts, tickets, mobile phones, pets and accessories, and clothes also appeared high on TSB’s most-scammed list.

In separate polling of 2,000 Brits, commissioned by TSB and carried out by Censuswide, it was revealed that 33% of 2,000 UK citizens have lost money to online purchase scams. It also showed that 41% of British people are not confident they can distinguish between AI-generated images and genuine photographs when shopping online. 

In September, National Trading Standards revealed that around half of UK citizens are finding it more difficult to tell genuine offers from scams as AI is increasingly being used to con people. According to the survey, 47% of UK adults struggle to tell what online offers are genuine or AI fakes. It also found that 24% feel “overwhelmed” by increasingly sophisticated scams.

The government agency launched its AI Scam Watchlist, “revealing the tools and techniques increasingly being used by criminals to supercharge their scams – from digital humans and cloned voices to deepfakes and AI-generated images – and setting out how consumers can protect themselves”.

In April 2025, banks and tech firms came together in an initiative to share information on fraud to give them visibility of attacks targeted at customers. The collaboration is part of Stop Scams UK’s intelligence-sharing pilots, which have brought together banks such as HSBC, NatWest and Santander with tech firms Amazon, Google and Meta.

Mobile telecommunications firm Three, BT, challenger bank Monzo, Lloyds Bank and tech giant Meta are among the members that published the Stop Scams UK joint statement.

According to the statement, this year presents a unique opportunity for collaboration. “Through Stop Scams UK, tech, telecoms companies and financial services providers have joined forces to share technology, data and intelligence to combat fraudsters on the platforms where they operate, helping to boost consumer confidence and promote economic growth,” it said.
